records.title: Qin Great Wall
records.summary: After unifying China in 221 BCE, the Qin sent general Meng Tian north with 300,000 troops; he drove back the Xiongnu and joined older Qin, Zhao and Yan walls into a line the Shiji says ran over 10,000 li.
records.card: Once Qin had conquered its rivals in 221 BCE, the First Emperor turned to the northern frontier. His general Meng Tian pushed the Xiongnu out of the lands south of the Yellow River bend, and soldiers, convicts and resettled families linked the separate northern walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan into one line from Lintao to Liaodong. Sima Qian, who later travelled the line, judged that it was built with little regard for the people's strength.
records.what:
The Qin Great Wall is the first attempt to join China's separate northern walls into a single frontier. Its main written source is the Shiji of the Han historian Sima Qian. In the biography of Meng Tian, once Qin had swallowed the other states, the First Emperor (Qin Shi Huang) sent Meng Tian north with 300,000 men to drive out the Rong and Di peoples and take the lands south of the Yellow River, then built a long wall that followed the terrain and used natural strongholds from Lintao in the west to Liaodong in the east, more than 10,000 li in all. Meng Tian's army stayed in the field for more than ten years, based in Shang commandery, and his reputation, the text says, overawed the Xiongnu.

The basic annals of the First Emperor give tighter dates. In the emperor's 32nd year (215 BCE) Meng Tian led 300,000 troops against the Hu and took the Henan lands; in the 33rd year (214 BCE) the Xiongnu were driven back, 34 new counties were set up along the river from Yuzhong toward the Yin Mountains, and walls were built on the river as a frontier; in the 34th year (213 BCE) officials judged to have administered justice unfairly were banished to build the long wall. In the 36th year (211 BCE) 30,000 households were moved to the northern river lands and Yuzhong. The two chapters disagree on when the northern campaign began, either soon after unification in 221 BCE or in 215 BCE.

Modern heritage bodies describe the work as linking and restoring walls that the states of Qin, Zhao and Yan had built in the 3rd century BCE, extended west along the Yellow River toward Lanzhou and finished shortly before the Han took power. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, a forged order in his name forced Meng Tian to take poison. China's 2012 survey counts 3,680.26 km of surviving Qin and Han walls together, without separating the two dynasties.

uncertainty.note: Start: Shiji 88 places Meng Tian's northern command after the unification of 221 BCE and says his army was in the field more than ten years; Shiji 6 dates the northern offensive to the First Emperor's 32nd year (215 BCE) and wall-building to 214–213 BCE. End: Meng Tian's death in 210 BCE; ICOMOS says the system was completed shortly before the Han (206 BCE).

records.how: The Qin did not build a new wall from nothing. ICOMOS describes the work as restoring and linking walls that Qin, Zhao and Yan had already built in the 3rd century BCE, and SACH's survey report likewise says the northern walls of the three states were connected. The sequence in the Shiji is military first: Meng Tian's army drove the Hu out of the Henan lands (215 BCE), Qin then founded new counties along the Yellow River and fortified the river itself as a frontier (214 BCE), crossed the river to hold Gaoque, Yangshan and Beijia, and built forts and watch posts to keep the Rong out. The wall itself followed the lie of the land, using cliffs, ridges and passes as part of the barrier. Labour combined the army, convicts and officials banished for unjust judgments, while the frontier was filled with exiles and, in 211 BCE, 30,000 resettled households. Surviving Qin and Han walls are mostly earth and stone. In 212 BCE the Straight Road was cut from Jiuyuan to Yunyang to move troops north. How many workers died is not recorded in any source opened for this record.
records.why_it_matters: This was the moment separate state walls became an imperial frontier. By joining the Qin, Zhao and Yan walls and fortifying the new river counties, Qin drew a line between the farming empire and the steppe that later dynasties, above all the Han, extended and rebuilt. In the short term it pushed the Xiongnu back: the Han writer Jia Yi, quoted by Sima Qian, claimed the Hu were driven more than 700 li away and no longer dared to graze their horses to the south. It also moved people: convicts, banished officials and 30,000 households were sent to the frontier. Its cost became part of the case against Qin. Sima Qian, writing under the Han, said Meng Tian had treated the people's strength lightly when the empire was newly united and its wounds unhealed, and he rejected Meng Tian's own deathbed claim that his only crime was cutting the veins of the earth. Had Qin not taken and walled the Henan lands, the Xiongnu would have kept pastures within easy reach of the Qin heartland, and the early Han, which faced a powerful Xiongnu confederation, would have inherited a weaker northern frontier.

records.title: Classical Athens (508/507–322 BCE)
records.summary: From Cleisthenes' reforms of 508/507 BCE to a Macedonian-imposed property franchise in 322 BCE, Athens was a direct democracy of adult male citizens that led a naval league, built the Parthenon and fostered drama and philosophy, while excluding women, metics and enslaved people.
records.card: For almost two centuries the Athenians governed themselves through an open assembly, a council of 500 chosen by lot and large citizen juries. Victory over Persia and tribute from the Delian League paid for a fleet and the Acropolis buildings, but war with Sparta, plague and the killings of the Thirty followed. Only adult men with two Athenian parents could vote; by one estimate roughly 250,000 inhabitants lived in Attica in 431 BCE, while more than 30,000 enslaved men worked in the silver mines and fleet alone.
records.what:
Classical Athens here means the period from the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/507 BCE to 322 BCE, when the Macedonian regent Antipater, after Athens' defeat in the Lamian War, replaced the democracy with a franchise limited by wealth. The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians places Cleisthenes' measures in the archonship of Isagoras: he replaced the four old tribes with ten, each drawn from city, coastal and inland districts, enlarged the council to 500 members, fifty per tribe, and made the deme the basis of citizenship. Ostracism, a vote on potsherds requiring a quorum of 6,000 votes, was first used two years after Marathon; whether Cleisthenes himself introduced it is debated.

The Athenians defeated a Persian force at Marathon in 490 BCE. Silver from the mines at Maronea paid for 100 triremes, and in 480 BCE the Persians sacked the Acropolis before that fleet fought at Salamis. In 478 BCE Athens formed the Delian League of about 140 cities; its treasury moved from Delos to Athens in 454 BCE. A law proposed by Pericles in 451/450 BCE restricted citizenship to children of two Athenian parents, and the Parthenon was built between 447 and 438 BCE, its pedimental sculpture finished in 432 BCE. At the Great Dionysia the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides competed.

The Peloponnesian War with Sparta (431–404 BCE), during which plague struck Athens from 430 BCE, ended in defeat. The Spartan-backed Thirty put at least 1,500 people to death before democracy was restored in 404/403 BCE. Socrates was tried and executed in 399 BCE; Plato founded the Academy around 387 BCE and Aristotle the Lyceum in 335/334 BCE. Philip II's victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE made Macedon supreme in Greece.

Political rights belonged only to adult male citizens; women, metics (free resident foreigners who paid an annual tax) and enslaved people had none. Demographers estimate at least 60,000 male citizens and roughly 250,000 total inhabitants in 431 BCE, while more than 30,000 enslaved men worked in the mines and navy alone; no ancient source counted women.

uncertainty.note: Start: the archon year of Isagoras ran from midsummer 508 to midsummer 507 BCE, so the reforms fall in 508 or 507 BCE (astronomical -507 or -506). End: Antipater's settlement followed the Athenian defeat at Crannon, dated by Dinsmoor to 5 September 322 BCE (Geer's Loeb note); Diodorus files these events under the archon year 323/2, a known chronological confusion. Choosing 508/507–322 BCE as bounds is a convention: it brackets the democracy rather than the art-historical 'Classical period'.

records.how: The democracy rested on structures Cleisthenes built after the Peisistratid tyranny ended: ten tribes that each combined demes from the city, the coast and the inland districts, a council of 500 drawn from the tribes, and registration in a deme as proof of citizenship. Over the fifth century, power passed further to ordinary citizens. Most offices were filled by lot for a single year; the assembly on the Pnyx passed laws, elected generals and decided on war and peace; juries of citizens heard cases, allotted to courts by stone machines (kleroteria), and Aristotle records juror pay as half a drachma a day. Sea power drove the rest. On Themistocles' proposal, silver from Maronea became a fleet of 100 triremes that fought at Salamis. Athens then led the Delian League, collected tribute first assessed by Aristides, moved the league treasury to Athens in 454 BCE and paid citizens and foreigners a drachma a day to build on the Acropolis. Allies that revolted, such as Thasos (465–463 BCE) and Samos (441–439 BCE), had to pull down their walls and surrender their fleets. Rivalry with Sparta led to the war of 431–404 BCE, in which Pericles' strategy brought the Athenians inside the city walls and relied on the navy. Defeat, the rule of the Thirty and Macedonian expansion followed, and in 322 BCE Antipater's 2,000-drachma property qualification removed more than 12,000 poorer men from the citizen body.
records.why_it_matters: Classical Athens is the best-documented early state run directly by its ordinary citizens, and its working parts survive as physical evidence: ostraka, allotment tokens, ballots and kleroteria excavated in the Agora. The same city produced the surviving canon of Greek tragedy, the Parthenon, the history of Thucydides and the schools of Plato and Aristotle; the Academy lasted until the emperor Justinian closed it in 529 CE. Its limits matter as much. The franchise excluded all women, resident foreigners and enslaved people, and the wealth that paid citizens for public service came partly from allied tribute and from slave labour, with more than 30,000 enslaved men estimated to have been needed in the silver mines and the fleet alone. Defeat in 404 BCE and the killings by the Thirty showed how quickly the system could be overturned, and the restored democracy's execution of Socrates deepened Plato's distrust of its institutions. A counterfactual shows how contingent the period was: had the Assembly shared out the Maronea silver instead of building triremes, Athens would have met the Persian invasion of 480 BCE without the fleet that fought at Salamis, and without the naval league whose tribute later funded the Acropolis buildings. The end came by force, not decay: in 322 BCE a Macedonian property qualification stripped more than 12,000 poorer Athenians of their citizenship, leaving about 9,000 men in control of the city.

records.title: Rise of Rome (Republic to Empire)
records.summary: Between the traditional founding of the Republic in 509 BCE and Augustus's settlement of 27 BCE, the city-state of Rome conquered Italy, destroyed Carthage, absorbed Greece and much of western Asia, and turned through civil war into a monarchy ruling the Mediterranean.
records.card: Rome grew from Iron Age huts by the Tiber into a city ruled first by kings and then, by the traditional reckoning from 509 BCE, by an aristocratic republic. Over the next five centuries it subdued Italy, won three wars against Carthage and took over the Greek east, enslaving hundreds of thousands of people as it went. The strains of that empire wrecked the Republic in a century of political killings and civil wars, from which Caesar's heir Octavian emerged as sole ruler, renamed Augustus in 27 BCE.
records.what:
Roman tradition said that Romulus founded the city on the Palatine Hill in 753 BCE; UNESCO and modern scholars present that date as legend. Archaeology shows a hut settlement instead: the Metropolitan Museum dates the first cluster of huts to the 10th century BCE, while the post-holes cut into the Palatine bedrock are dated by Diana Kleiner of Yale to the 8th century BCE. Kings ruled the early city, the later ones Etruscan; from 509 BCE, by the conventional chronology, a republic of elected magistrates replaced them. A long contest between the patrician aristocracy and the plebeians ended in 287 BCE with a mixed patrician-plebeian nobility.

Polybius describes expansion in stages. After recovering from a Gallic capture of the city, the Romans subdued the Latins, Etruscans, Samnites and Italian Celts and drove out Pyrrhus, making most of Italy subject to them. In 264 BCE they crossed to Sicily, opening three Punic Wars against Carthage (264–241, 218–201 and 149–146 BCE). Hannibal invaded Italy across the Alps and crushed a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BCE, but Scipio Africanus defeated him at Zama in 202 BCE. Polybius, writing in Greek, marvelled that Rome brought nearly the whole known world under its rule in under 53 years from the Hannibalic war. In 167 BCE, after the defeat of Macedon, Roman troops sacked Epirus and, by the ancient count, sold 150,000 people into slavery; in 146 BCE Carthage was razed and its land became the province of Africa.

Conquest brought wealth, captives and widening inequality. The killing of the tribune Tiberius Gracchus in 133 BCE began a century of political violence: the Social War with Rome's Italian allies from 91 BCE, the slave revolt led by Spartacus from 73 BCE and the wars of the great generals. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, accepted the dictatorship for life and was stabbed to death at a senate meeting on 15 March 44 BCE. His heir Octavian defeated his rivals, finally at Actium in 31 BCE, and in January 27 BCE the senate named him Augustus. Sources disagree over the founding (legend versus excavation) and over how far Augustus restored or replaced the Republic.

uncertainty.note: 509 BCE is the conventional (Varronian) date for the end of the monarchy, inherited from Roman annalistic chronology and not independently fixed; early Republican dates may be off by several years. The end date is secure: the senate's grant of the name Augustus, dated by the Loeb editor of the Res Gestae to 16 January 27 BCE (Julian calendar). The traditional founding of the city (753 BCE) is legendary and is not used as the record's start.

records.how: Polybius explains the first phase as a sequence of wars fought outward from Latium: once Rome had subdued the Latins, Etruscans, Samnites and Italian Celts and expelled Pyrrhus, it controlled the manpower of most of Italy, and the war over Sicily from 264 BCE drew it into a contest with Carthage at sea. Victory over Hannibal, in Polybius's reading, convinced the Romans that they could reach for Greece and Asia, and the defeat of Macedon in 168 BCE was followed by exemplary terror in Epirus in 167 BCE. Conquered land outside Italy was organised as provinces paying tribute; Caesar alone imposed 40 million sesterces a year on Gaul, according to Suetonius. Wars also fed a vast trade in captives: Scheidel models an inflow of 2 to 4 million slaves into Italy over the last two centuries BCE. Wealth flowed unevenly, and the Met attributes the Republic's collapse to the strain of permanent military commitment and the gulf between those who profited and those impoverished. The Gracchi tried to redistribute public land through a three-man commission and were killed in 133 and 121 BCE. The Social War of 91–88 BCE forced Rome to extend citizenship to its Italian allies. Commanders whose soldiers looked to them for reward then fought one another; Caesar's dictatorship ended in his assassination, and Octavian, who had raised a private army at nineteen, finished the civil wars and in 28–27 BCE recast his power as a restored republic under his leadership.
records.why_it_matters: This process created the state that, in UNESCO's words, dominated the Mediterranean world for many centuries, with Rome as its capital. By 27 BCE a single city governed provinces from Spain to Syria and from Gaul to Africa, and its Augustan census counted 4,063,000 citizens in 28 BCE. UNESCO credits the city with spreading law, language and literature that became the basis of Western culture. The same expansion ended other worlds: Carthage, the capital of Punic civilization in Africa, was razed in 146 BCE, and wars of conquest moved an estimated 2 to 4 million captives into slavery in Italy in the last two centuries BCE alone. The Republic's failure also produced a new political form: Augustus presented his monarchy as a restored republic in which he merely outranked his colleagues, while the Met describes his position as complete control. A counterfactual shows how contingent this was: had Hannibal's victories after Cannae in 216 BCE broken Rome's hold on Italy, the western Mediterranean would probably have remained divided between Punic and Roman spheres, and the rapid absorption of the Greek east that Polybius dated from the Hannibalic war could not have followed. Without the political violence that began with Tiberius Gracchus, the Republic might have absorbed its empire through institutions rather than through warlords, and the Principate need not have emerged in the form Augustus gave it.

related.because: The territorial empire assembled between 509 and 27 BCE, and the one-man rule Augustus built over it, became the state whose western provinces fragmented between 376 and 476 CE.

perspectives.holder: Archaeological evidence, summarised by the Metropolitan Museum and by Diana Kleiner
perspectives.account: Rome began as a cluster of Iron Age huts; the Met dates the first huts to the 10th century BCE, and Kleiner describes post-hole huts cut into the Palatine tufa in the 8th century BCE, with hut-shaped cremation urns as supporting evidence.

perspectives.holder: Augustus, Res Gestae 34 (written AD 14)
perspectives.account: After ending the civil wars he handed the state back to the senate and people in 28–27 BCE, and thereafter outranked others in prestige but held no more formal power than his colleagues in office.

perspectives.holder: Metropolitan Museum of Art (modern historical summary)
perspectives.account: Octavian removed all opposition to his complete control of the Roman state before receiving the title Augustus in 27 BCE; the Republic had collapsed under the strains of empire.

perspectives.account: Many, though not all, Epirote settlements survived the 167 BCE destructions, so the ancient picture of total devastation needs qualifying; the enslavement figure itself cannot be checked archaeologically.

records.title: Agricultural (Neolithic) revolution
records.summary: From about 12,000 years ago, people in at least eleven separate regions of the world began cultivating plants and herding animals, slowly turning wild species into crops and livestock and laying the economic foundation of villages, towns and states.
records.card: Farming was not invented once. In the Fertile Crescent, wild cereals were being managed by about 12,000 years ago, and similar transitions followed independently in China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, the African Sahel and eastern North America. Each took thousands of years, and scholars still debate why it happened when it did and whether it made people's lives better or worse.
records.what:
The agricultural or Neolithic revolution is the shift, across many parts of the world, from living only on wild plants and animals to cultivating crops and keeping livestock. The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe introduced the idea of a prehistoric revolution in 1934 and popularised it in his 1936 book Man Makes Himself, picturing a single transformation that began with grain growing in Mesopotamia and spread outward.

Later evidence has replaced that picture with many separate beginnings. A 2014 review by Larson and 23 colleagues counts at least 11 regions of the Old and New Worlds as independent centres of domestication, with several more proposed. In the Fertile Crescent of southwest Asia, people were intensively managing wild cereals by about 12,000 calibrated years before present (cal BP), but non-shattering, domesticated cereal ears are not well established until about 10,500 cal BP; sheep, goats, pigs and cattle came under management between about 11,000 and 10,000 cal BP. In northern China, common millet was stored at Cishan, Hebei, from about 10,300 cal BP; in the Lower Yangtze, rice phytoliths at Shangshan, Zhejiang, show domestication beginning by about 9,400 cal BP. Maize was being processed at Xihuatoxtla shelter in Mexico's Central Balsas Valley by 8,700 cal BP. In the Andean foothills of northern Peru, people at Ñanchoc were eating squash, peanuts and beans by about 8,600 cal BP. At Kuk in highland New Guinea, cultivation mounds for bananas, taro and yam date to about 7,000–6,400 years ago. In eastern North America, local squash, sunflower, marshelder and chenopod were domesticated between about 5,000 and 3,700 cal BP, and fully domesticated pearl millet appears in southeastern Mali by about 2500 BCE.

The process was slow: in wheat, barley and rice the non-shattering trait took roughly 2,000–4,000 years to become fixed. Its causes are disputed. Climate change, population pressure and competitive feasting have all been proposed, and many researchers now doubt that any single cause explains every centre.

uncertainty.note: Start = intensified management of wild plants in the Fertile Crescent, 'at least' c. 12,000 cal BP (Zeder 2008); Larson et al. (2014) place the beginning of domestication 12,000–11,000 years ago. End is a convention: the latest primary centre dated in this record (chenopod in eastern North America, c. 3,700 cal BP intercept, Smith 2006); Larson et al. note that most domesticates arose in the middle Holocene, 7,000–4,000 BP, and domestication of new species has never fully stopped. Conversion: year = 1950 − cal BP.

records.how: There was no single sequence, but the best-studied centres share a pattern. (1) Foragers began to manage wild resources intensively: in the Fertile Crescent, wild cereal management goes back at least to about 12,000 cal BP, and Larson and colleagues describe a phase of predomestication cultivation documented in the Near East, China and northwestern South America. (2) Repeated sowing and harvesting selected for traits useful to people, above all ears that do not shatter; in wheat, barley and rice that trait took roughly 2,000–4,000 years to become fixed, and claims of domestication within 100–200 years have been questioned. (3) Animal management grew out of hunting strategies: in the Fertile Crescent sheep and goats were managed from about 11,000–10,500 cal BP, pigs from 10,500–10,000 and cattle from 11,000–10,000, but clear changes in bone size appear only around 9,500–9,000 cal BP. (4) Crops and herds then combined into mixed farming economies, which crystallised in the Fertile Crescent around 9,500–9,000 cal BP and spread with colonists to Cyprus (10,500–9,000 cal BP), the Aegean (9,000–8,000), Italy (c. 8,000) and the coasts of Iberia (7,700–7,300). Elsewhere the order differed: in the Americas crops were domesticated before animals, while in parts of Africa, Arabia and India animals came first. The triggers proposed include the end of the Younger Dryas cold, dry interval at about 11,700 years ago and the more stable Holocene that followed, population growth, and feasting, for which Göbekli Tepe offers evidence on a large scale.
records.why_it_matters: Farming changed how many people the land could feed and how they lived. A farming family typically raised more children than a foraging one, and mixed crop-and-livestock economies supported dense, year-round settlements: Çatalhöyük in Anatolia held perhaps 3,500–8,000 people at its peak in the 7th millennium BCE. The plants and animals domesticated in this period, among them wheat, barley, rice, millets, maize, squash, bananas, taro, sheep, goats, pigs and cattle, are still farmed today. Farming also spread people: colonist farmers carried the Neolithic way of life from southwest Asia to Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Iberia over about three thousand years, while Late Mesolithic forager populations there declined. The change had costs. At Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, crowding, poor sanitation and starchy diets brought infections, tooth decay and more interpersonal violence, and researchers see similar health costs in early farming societies worldwide, although a 2023 study found that much of the decline in human stature began before farming. Because farming arose independently at least eleven times, its story is not only about southwest Asia: the bananas and taro of New Guinea and the millets of the Sahel were domesticated by their own people. Had people everywhere remained foragers, human numbers would have stayed smaller and settlement more mobile, and the permanent villages on which later towns and cities were built would not have existed in the same form.

perspectives.holder: V. Gordon Childe (1934; Man Makes Himself, 1936), as summarised by Frieman (2020)
perspectives.account: Farming was a revolution comparable to the Industrial Revolution: a sudden economic change that began with grain cultivation in Mesopotamia and spread outward, transforming each society it reached.

perspectives.holder: Larson et al. (2014); Zeder (2008); Frieman (2020)
perspectives.account: Domestication was protracted and plural: crops were domesticated many times in at least 11 regions, cultivation of wild plants preceded visible domestication by centuries to millennia, and key traits took 2,000–4,000 years to fix, so the change was not a single sudden event.

perspectives.holder: Larson et al. (2014); Lu et al. (2009)
perspectives.account: Climate change is the main ecological backdrop: lower late-Pleistocene CO2 and temperatures limited plant productivity, and Holocene conditions made agriculture a more favourable strategy; in northern China a drier early Holocene may have favoured common millet.

perspectives.holder: Regattieri et al. (2025), from a Kurdistan speleothem record
perspectives.account: Climate cannot be used deterministically: the Zagros was largely unoccupied in the drier Younger Dryas, and permanent settlement appeared near its end, but neolithization there reworked earlier forager traditions once conditions stabilised.

perspectives.holder: Göbekli Tepe excavators (Dietrich, Heun, Notroff, Schmidt, Zarnkow 2012), building on Hayden's feasting model
perspectives.account: Large ritual gatherings and feasts among hunter-gatherers demanded food, and perhaps beer from wild cereals, which may have encouraged cereal cultivation near Karacadağ; the authors note that brewing at the site is not yet proven.

perspectives.holder: Shavit and Sharon (2023); Larson et al. (2014)
perspectives.account: Single-cause explanations (climate, population growth, technology, property or a cognitive shift) are unsatisfying; different causes may have operated in different centres.

perspectives.holder: Larsen et al. (2019), Çatalhöyük bioarchaeology
perspectives.account: Farming and dense settlement carried clear health costs worldwide: at Çatalhöyük, infection, dental caries, heavier workloads and interpersonal violence accompanied crowding and cereal-rich diets.

perspectives.holder: Stock et al. (2023), stature of 3,507 skeletons from 366 sites
perspectives.account: Declining stature and body mass mostly began before agriculture, mean stature bottomed out between 8,000 and 6,000 years ago, and regions of local domestication such as the Levant and China were relatively stable, so farming alone does not explain shrinking bodies.

records.title: Breakup of Pangaea
records.summary: From about 201 million years ago the supercontinent Pangaea came apart: the Central Atlantic opened amid the CAMP flood basalts, Laurasia and Gondwana separated, the South Atlantic unzipped, and India drifted north into Asia.
records.card: Pangaea, welded together when Gondwana and Laurussia collided in the late Paleozoic, began rifting in the Triassic and split apart from about 201 million years ago. The first break ran between North America and northwest Africa, where the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted at the same moment as the end-Triassic mass extinction. Over the next 150 million years the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans opened and India crossed the Tethys to meet Asia.
records.what:
Pangaea was the supercontinent that gathered almost all of Earth's continental crust in the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic. It assembled as the Rheic Ocean closed: Gondwana and Laurussia were largely joined by the Mississippian, and West Africa and South America sutured onto North America during the Carboniferous and early Permian, raising the Variscan, Alleghanian and Ouachita mountain belts in collisions spanning roughly 380 to 290 million years ago (Ma). The last additions, the North and South China blocks, docked in the Triassic.

Breakup had a long run-up. Rifts began opening inside Pangaea around 240 Ma, and by the end of the Triassic rift basins such as the Fundy, Newark and Argana basins lined the future margins of eastern North America and Morocco. About 201.5 Ma the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) erupted and intruded across this rift zone and far beyond it, from the Amazon basin to Iberia; a 1999 study estimated its extent at about 7 million km² and its magma volume at about 2 million km³. High-precision zircon dates place the first CAMP pulses at the same time as the end-Triassic mass extinction, about 201.56 Ma, although whether the eruptions caused the extinction is still argued.

Seafloor spreading then separated North America from northwest Africa, cutting the northern landmass, Laurasia, from the southern one, Gondwana. When spreading began is disputed: older models put the oldest Central Atlantic ocean crust in the Middle Jurassic, while reinterpretations of magnetic anomalies and salt basins push it back to about 195–190 Ma. Gondwana split into eastern and western halves in the Early Jurassic. Between about 140 and 103 Ma South America and Africa pulled apart from south to north, opening the South Atlantic. Greater India left Australia–Antarctica around 136–126 Ma and Madagascar around 94–84 Ma, then moved rapidly north and collided with Asia about 50–40 Ma.

Alfred Wegener argued from 1912 that the continents had once been joined and later named the supercontinent Pangaea; confirming evidence arrived only from the mid-1950s.

uncertainty.note: Start is set at the CAMP eruptions and end-Triassic extinction (c. 201.5 Ma), the conventional moment of breakup; intracontinental rifting began c. 240 Ma (Müller et al. 2019). Onset of Central Atlantic seafloor spreading is disputed (c. 195–190 Ma vs Middle Jurassic). End is set at India's collision with Asia, dated 50–40 Ma; plate motion continues today.

paleo.plate_model: MERDITH2021 (Merdith et al. 2021, palaeomagnetic reference frame) via GPlates Web Service
paleo.note: Old Wife pin at 201 Ma. Model spread is large: MULLER2019 gives 10.22 N, 10.89 W (mantle reference frame); PALEOMAP gives 26.89 N, 13.79 W. Whiteside et al. 2010 place the nearby Newark and Hartford rift basins at 19–20 N, consistent with MERDITH2021. Other region points at their dates (MERDITH2021): Argana 18.44 N, 0.85 E (201 Ma); Senador Pompeu 10.76 S, 3.46 E (201 Ma); Benguela 24.05 S, 4.00 E (113 Ma). India track, Nagpur (21.1463 N, 79.0849 E): 45.20 S at 130 Ma, 34.65 S at 80 Ma, 4.30 S at 50 Ma. The Mascarene Basin point is ocean floor younger than c. 94 Ma and has no meaningful earlier position.

records.how: Breakup was driven by extension of the continental lithosphere. From about 240 Ma Pangaea stretched along networks of rifts; by the latest Triassic, fault-bounded basins such as Fundy, Newark and Argana had filled with river, lake and dune sediments. Around 201.5 Ma huge volumes of basaltic magma rose into and through these basins and far beyond them as dykes, sills and lava flows: the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Its main eruptive phase lasted a few hundred thousand years, and gases released from the magma and from heated carbon-rich basin sediments are the leading explanation for the end-Triassic extinction. Continental crust then gave way to new ocean crust formed at a mid-ocean ridge. In one model, Central Atlantic spreading ran very slowly (about 0.8 cm a year) for its first 20 million years, sped up to about 1.7 cm a year after a change of direction at about 170 Ma, and produced more crust on the American side. Breakup was diachronous elsewhere: the South Atlantic rift extended slowly east–west from 140 Ma, localised strain from about 126 Ma, and broke up from south to north between about 113 and 103 Ma. In the east, a ridge between Greater India and Australia–Antarctica propagated from about 136 Ma, and after a reorganisation near 100 Ma India separated from Madagascar. India's northward motion, about 9 cm a year near 80 Ma, closed the Tethys and ended in collision with Asia. Wegener could not name a force able to move continents, the main objection raised against him; plate tectonics later supplied one.
records.why_it_matters: The breakup of Pangaea made the map of the modern world. It opened the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, set the Americas apart from Africa and Europe, isolated Antarctica, Australia and India, and by the end of the Cretaceous had brought most continents close to their present shapes. Its opening act, the CAMP eruptions, coincides with the end-Triassic mass extinction, which removed roughly half of marine species and cleared the way for dinosaurs to dominate land for the rest of the Mesozoic. Its closing act, India's collision with Asia, began raising the Himalaya, which still rise by more than 1 cm a year. The rifts left behind built the passive margins on both sides of the South Atlantic, including the pre-salt basins of Brazil and Angola. Without the breakup there would be no Atlantic Ocean between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia, no Himalaya, and the separate evolutionary histories of island continents such as Australia would not have unfolded the same way. The breakup also mattered for science: matching coastlines, fossils and rocks on opposite sides of the Atlantic led Wegener to propose continental drift in 1912, an idea rejected for decades that became a foundation of plate tectonics once seafloor evidence arrived from the mid-1950s. Today the record drives the Atlas's ambient Plates layer between about 240 and 50 Ma.

records.title: Peopling of the Americas
records.summary: The ancestors of Indigenous Americans came from northeast Asia by way of Beringia and spread to the tip of South America. Footprints in New Mexico suggest people were south of the ice sheets by about 23,000 years ago, a date still debated.
records.card: Genomes show that Indigenous Americans descend from a population that split from East Asians roughly 26,000–24,000 years ago and paused, probably near Beringia, before spreading south. How early that spread began is argued: White Sands footprints point to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, while sceptics see the main expansion only after 16,000 years ago. The Clovis-first model is gone, the coastal and inland routes are both still in play, and even the long-accepted Monte Verde site in Chile was challenged in 2026.
records.what:
The peopling of the Americas is the process by which humans first reached North and South America and spread through them. Genetic studies indicate that Indigenous Americans descend from one ancestral population that separated from East Asians about 26,100–23,900 years ago and then lived in isolation long enough for distinctive founder lineages to form, a pause called the Beringian standstill. Tamm and colleagues (2007) placed that isolation in Beringia, the land exposed between Siberia and Alaska when sea level was low; others note it could have been anywhere from the Lake Baikal region to Hokkaido. After the pause, people spread quickly: the founder lineages are spread evenly from north to south rather than nested.

For decades many archaeologists held that the makers of Clovis tools, now dated to 13,050–12,750 calibrated years before present (cal BP), were the first Americans. That model was abandoned as older sites were accepted and genomes showed earlier occupation. The infant Anzick-1, buried with Clovis tools in Montana about 12,700–12,550 cal BP, belonged to a population closely related to all Indigenous Americans and directly ancestral to many.

The starting date is contested. Human footprints at White Sands National Park, New Mexico, made by many teenagers and children on the shores of Ice Age Lake Otero, are bracketed by radiocarbon dates on seeds of the aquatic plant Ruppia cirrhosa of about 22,900–21,100 cal BP, inside the Last Glacial Maximum. Critics argued that the seeds could have absorbed old carbon and might be thousands of years too old; a 2023 study dated land-plant pollen from the same layers and got matching ages. Other specialists still put the main expansion after about 16,000 years ago, with the earliest securely dated sites after about 15,000. Monte Verde in southern Chile, dated to about 14,500 cal BP and long the strongest pre-Clovis site, was argued in 2026 to be mid-Holocene in age, a reading its excavators and other geoarchaeologists reject. Whether the first migrants used the Pacific coast, open by about 17,000 years ago, or an inland ice-free corridor is unresolved, and some Indigenous nations hold origin accounts that reject a migration from Asia.

uncertainty.note: Years converted from calibrated radiocarbon years before present (BP = before 1950) as year = 1950 − cal BP. Start = c. 23,000 cal BP, the earliest bracket of the White Sands footprints (Bennett et al. 2021: Ruppia seed ages 22.86 ± 0.32 to 21.13 ± 0.25 ka, N = 11; Pigati et al. 2023 pollen and OSL ages agree). start_plus_years 8000 covers the critics' alternative of c. 15,000–13,000 cal BP (Oviatt et al. 2022) and the view that expansion began only after ~16,000 years ago (Potter et al. 2018). End = c. 12,750 cal BP, the close of Clovis, by which time Clovis and Fishtail complexes span both continents; this end point is an editorial convention, not a recorded event. Pre-LGM claims older than 23 ka are not adopted here.

records.how: The process turned on ice and sea level. (1) During the last glaciation, sea level fell far enough to expose Beringia, a broad land connection between Siberia and Alaska; plant remains about 18,000 years old preserved in ash from a Devil Mountain eruption in Alaska match its last proposed opening. (2) In the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000–19,000 years ago, the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets coalesced, closing both the interior ice-free corridor and, in southeastern Alaska, the Pacific coast, where the ice margin peaked about 20,000–17,000 years ago. (3) Cut off, the ancestral population stood still: mitochondrial founder lineages A2, B2, C1, D1 and others accumulated mutations that separate them from their Asian sister lineages, and the Ancient Beringian branch split off about 22,000–18,000 years ago. (4) As ice retreated, the coast opened first: by about 17,000 years ago southeastern Alaska offered an open path with productive marine and land ecosystems. The interior corridor opened physically between about 15,600 and 14,800 years ago and became biologically viable by 13,000–12,600 years ago in one reading, or as early as 15,000–14,000 in another. (5) Once south of the ice, people spread rapidly: founder lineages appear across both continents, northern and southern branches split about 17,500–14,600 years ago, and Clovis in North America and Fishtail points in South America are continent-wide by 13,000–12,900 cal BP. If the White Sands dates are right, some people were already south of the ice before the LGM closed the routes, so the first crossing must predate the closure.
records.why_it_matters: This process produced the founding ancestry of Indigenous peoples across the Americas (later pulses of gene flow from Asia added to it among some northern groups) and set the stage for all later human history in the hemisphere: independent plant domestication, the Classic Maya, Tenochtitlan and Cusco all grew from populations whose roots lie in this dispersal. It also matters for how science works. The Clovis-first model, built on a narrow window of 13,050–12,750 cal BP, dominated for decades and was overturned by sites and genomes, and the same contest continues over White Sands and, since 2026, over Monte Verde. The dates decide basic questions. If the White Sands footprints are 23,000–21,000 years old, people were south of the ice before the Last Glacial Maximum closed both the coastal and interior routes, so the coast-versus-corridor debate would concern later movements rather than the first arrival; had the footprints instead been 15,000–13,000 years old, as critics proposed, they would fit the older consensus of expansion after 16,000 years ago. At White Sands, people and megafauna shared the lakeshore for at least two millennia, which bears on whether people drove late Pleistocene extinctions. Finally, the research touches living communities. The Anzick-1 genome was studied after consultation with several tribal nations, many of whose representatives asked for reburial, and Indigenous scholars and elders have argued that framing their ancestors simply as migrants can be used to weaken ties to land.

related.because: The dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa and across Asia produced the northeast Asian population from which the ancestors of Native Americans separated about 26,000–24,000 years ago.

related.title: Last Glacial Maximum
related.because: Lowered sea level during the glaciation exposed the Beringian land bridge, while coalesced ice sheets closed the routes south and are thought to have isolated the founding population in the Beringian standstill.
By settling both continents, the first Americans established the populations whose descendants later developed farming independently in the Americas, without contact with the Old World centres.

perspectives.holder: Bennett, Bustos, Pigati, Springer and colleagues (Science 2021, 2022 reply, 2023); USGS and NPS
perspectives.account: Footprints at White Sands Locality 2 are bracketed by seed ages of about 23,000–21,000 cal BP, and terrestrial pollen and luminescence dates from the same layers agree, so people were south of the ice sheets during the Last Glacial Maximum.

perspectives.holder: Madsen et al. (Science comment, 2022); Oviatt, Madsen, Rhode and Davis (Quaternary Research, 2022)
perspectives.account: Ruppia is an aquatic plant that takes up old dissolved carbon; living Ruppia collected in 1947 gave an apparent age of about 7,400 years, so the footprints could be roughly 15,000–13,000 years old. They called for pollen and luminescence dating, which the 2023 study then supplied.

perspectives.holder: Potter and colleagues (Science Advances, 2018)
perspectives.account: Genetic and archaeological data put ancestral Native American expansion after about 16,000 years ago, with the earliest securely dated sites after about 15,000; both a coastal and an interior route remain viable and neither can yet be rejected.

perspectives.holder: Lesnek, Briner and colleagues (Science Advances, 2018)
perspectives.account: The ice-free corridor was not biologically viable until about 13,000 or 12,600 years ago, too late for the first migrants; the southeastern Alaska coast was open and productive after about 17,000 years ago and is the more likely early route.

perspectives.holder: Clovis-first model (dominant for decades; now abandoned, as described by Waters et al. 2020 and Rasmussen et al. 2014)
perspectives.account: The makers of Clovis tools were the first people in the Americas. Sites older than Clovis, Western Stemmed points as old as or older than Clovis, a Fishtail complex established in South America by about 12,900 cal BP, and genetic evidence for earlier occupation have overturned this view.

perspectives.holder: Dillehay and colleagues (PLOS ONE 2015; Science eLetter 2026); UNESCO Tentative List entry (Chile, 2004)
perspectives.account: Monte Verde II is a securely dated camp of about 14,500–14,800 cal BP, and scattered horizons at the nearby MV-I and Chinchihuapi localities may reach about 18,500 cal BP.

perspectives.holder: Surovell, Méndez, García, Lüthgens, Thompson and Latorre (Science, March 2026)
perspectives.account: Alluvial dates and an approximately 11,000-year-old tephra beneath the archaeological layer mean Monte Verde can be no older than the Middle Holocene, about 8,200–4,200 years BP, so it no longer anchors an early arrival in South America.

perspectives.holder: Waters, Halligan, Mandel, Holcomb, Davis and Holliday (Science eLetter, May 2026); Fundación Monte Verde
perspectives.account: Waters and colleagues argue the 2026 study mis-correlated its terrace deposits with the site stratigraphy, that its tephra may not be the Lepué Tephra, and that its own OSL ages show the creek surface existed by about 18,000–14,300 years ago. The foundation adds that the authors spent only hours on site and relied on non-archaeological deposits; both hold that the ~14,500-year age stands.

perspectives.holder: Indigenous voices reported by CBC News (2018): Willard Martin (Nisga'a elder), Oscar Dennis (Tahltan language conservationist), Woodrow Morrison (Haida elder), Paulette Steeves (Cree-Métis archaeologist)
perspectives.account: Martin said the Bering Strait account conflicts with Nisga'a oral history and origin stories; Dennis accepts a migration from Asia but by watercraft and reads origin stories as records of it; Morrison sees movement in several directions; Steeves argues the evidence for a single founding population is limited and that a Bering-only story is a colonial framing.

records.title: Permian–Triassic mass extinction
records.summary: About 251.9 million years ago, within roughly 60,000 years, most marine species and many land plants and animals died out: Earth's most severe known mass extinction, most likely set off by Siberian Traps magmatism and the warming it drove.
records.card: The end-Permian extinction, often called the Great Dying, is dated at Meishan in southeast China to between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago. Gases from the Siberian Traps, above all from magma sills baking carbon-rich basin sediments, are the leading suspect, with warming, oxygen loss and ocean acidification doing the killing. Recent estimates put marine species loss near 81%, lower than the 90–96% long quoted.
records.what:
The Permian–Triassic (end-Permian) mass extinction is the largest loss of life in the Phanerozoic fossil record and the event that closes the Paleozoic Era. Its best-dated record is the Meishan section in Changxing County, Zhejiang Province, China, where volcanic ash beds interleaved with marine limestones and mudstones have been dated by uranium–lead (U-Pb) analysis of zircon crystals. Burgess and colleagues (2014) placed the onset of extinction at the base of Bed 25, 251.941 ± 0.037 million years ago (Ma), and the end of the main extinction interval at Bed 28, 251.880 ± 0.031 Ma, a duration of about 61,000 ± 48,000 years. The formal Permian–Triassic boundary, defined by the first appearance of the conodont Hindeodus parvus at the base of Bed 27c and ratified as a global stratotype in 2001, falls inside that interval at 251.902 ± 0.024 Ma, the age shown on the International Chronostratigraphic Chart (v2024/12).

A sharp drop in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in marine carbonate, starting roughly 60,000 years before the die-off, records a large injection of isotopically light carbon into the ocean and atmosphere, and tropical sea-surface temperatures rose by about 10 °C. The prime suspect is the Siberian Traps, a large igneous province in northern Asia whose lavas, ash and intrusions total roughly 2–5 million km³. Lavas began erupting about 300,000 years before the extinction, but the extinction's onset matches the start of widespread sill intrusion into the sedimentary rocks of the Tunguska Basin.

Marine animals bore the brunt: heavily calcified organisms and species living far from the tropics were hit hardest. Estimates of the toll depend on method. The widely repeated figure of 90–96% of marine species comes from rarefaction work of 1979–1986; Stanley (2016), after separating out the earlier end-Guadalupian crisis and background extinction, estimated about 81% of marine species and 62% of genera. Whether the land extinction was simultaneous is also debated, because a 2020 date from South Africa's Karoo Basin places the classic vertebrate turnover there more than 300,000 years before the marine event.

uncertainty.note: 2-sigma analytical (internal) uncertainties from U-Pb zircon CA-ID-TIMS dates at Meishan (Burgess et al. 2014); tracer-calibration (0.03%) and U-238 decay-constant (0.05%) systematic uncertainties are additional. Duration 61 ± 48 kyr (abstract rounds to 60 ± 48 kyr). Carbon-cycle volatility continued for at least 500 kyr after onset.

records.how: The favoured chain runs from magma to dead oceans. (1) Siberian Traps magmatism began with explosive eruptions and then floods of lava; this first, lava-dominated stage, about two-thirds of the lava volume (more than 1 million km³), started just before 252.24 ± 0.1 Ma and caused little measurable disruption of the carbon cycle. (2) At 251.907 ± 0.067 Ma, overlapping the extinction onset within uncertainty, eruption largely gave way to the intrusion of sills across more than 1.5 million km² of the Tunguska Basin; their heat cooked evaporite, carbonate and hydrocarbon-bearing sediments and probably released very large volumes of carbon dioxide and methane. Burgess and Bowring judged this contact-metamorphism model the most plausible, and found the plume thermal-erosion and nickel-fed methanogen hypotheses less consistent with the timing. (3) The rapid release of isotopically light carbon produced the carbon-isotope excursion and greenhouse warming of roughly 10 °C in tropical surface waters. (4) Warmer water holds less oxygen while animals need more: an Earth-system model reproducing the proxy record depletes global marine oxygen by almost 80%, leaves about half the seafloor anoxic, and implies that temperature-dependent hypoxia accounts for more than half the extinction's magnitude, worst at high latitudes. (5) Boron-isotope pH records show stable pH during a first phase of slow carbon input, then an abrupt acidification during a second, rapid carbon pulse that removed heavily calcified species. (6) Carbon-cycle instability lasted at least 500,000 years, and Siberian magmatism continued for at least 500,000 years after the extinction.
records.why_it_matters: This extinction closes the Paleozoic Era: the base of the Triassic, defined at Meishan, is also the base of the Mesozoic, so the familiar sequence of Earth's eras turns on it. By removing roughly four in five marine species and around three in five marine genera, it reset ocean ecosystems, and the Triassic world that followed was rebuilt from a minority of surviving lineages, including the conodonts whose first appearance now marks the boundary. On land, the Gondwanan glossopterid floras and the Daptocephalus fauna gave way to new assemblages, although the exact timing of that change is still argued. The event also matters as the clearest test in the rock record of what happens when large amounts of carbon enter the atmosphere quickly. Its dating shows that the killing was a matter of tens of thousands of years, not millions, and its mechanism links greenhouse warming to oxygen loss and acidification in the sea. Penn and colleagues explicitly connect it to the ocean deoxygenation already under way today. The timing work also carries a counterfactual: in the Burgess reconstruction, the first 300,000 years of Siberian lavas did little damage, and the crisis began only when sills started baking carbon-rich sediments, so had the magma not intruded those volatile-rich basin rocks, the same eruption might have passed with far smaller losses. Without the extinction, the Mesozoic world would have been assembled from a very different and far larger pool of Paleozoic lineages.

related.title: Early Triassic biotic recovery
related.because: By removing about 81% of marine species and destabilising the carbon cycle for at least 500,000 years, the extinction forced Triassic ecosystems to be rebuilt from a minority of surviving lineages.

beats.action: chart.curve { field: d13C_carbonate, site: meishan }
beats.caption: At Meishan, carbon isotopes begin to swing toward lighter values about 60,000 years before the die-off: a sign of light carbon entering the ocean and air.

beats.action: region.pulse { region: tunguska-basin-sills, area_km2: 1500000 }
beats.caption: Close to the extinction's onset, eruption gives way to sills spreading through Tunguska Basin sediments; their heat likely releases huge volumes of CO2 and methane.

beats.action: camera.fly { to: [31.0798, 119.7058], show: 'Meishan Beds 25-28', paleo_model: MERDITH2021 }
beats.caption: Between Beds 25 and 28 at Meishan, about 61,000 ± 48,000 years, the main extinction unfolds. Timing compressed for display.

beats.action: layer.ocean { field: sst_and_o2, sst_delta_c: 10, o2_loss_pct: 80, reconstruction: model }
beats.caption: Model view: tropical surface waters warm by about 10 °C and the ocean loses almost 80% of its oxygen, emptying habitat for oxygen-hungry, high-latitude species.

beats.action: layer.ocean { field: ph, event: abrupt_drop }
beats.caption: A second, faster carbon pulse acidifies the ocean abruptly, removing heavily calcified marine organisms.

beats.action: marker.pin { at: [31.0798, 119.7058], label: 'Base of Triassic, Bed 27c' }
beats.caption: 251.902 ± 0.024 million years ago: the conodont Hindeodus parvus first appears, the agreed marker for the start of the Triassic and the Mesozoic.

beats.action: numbers.counter { field: marine_species_loss, range: [81, 96], unit: percent }
beats.caption: By the end, an estimated 81% of marine species are gone by Stanley's 2016 count; older estimates said 90–96%. The Paleozoic world of the seas is over.

beats.action: chart.curve { field: d13C_carbonate, label: 'carbon-cycle volatility >= 500 kyr' }
beats.caption: Carbon-cycle swings continue for at least half a million years, and Siberian magmatism keeps going long after the main die-off.

perspectives.account: After subtracting background extinction and removing losses that belong to the earlier end-Guadalupian crisis, about 81% of marine species (80.5–81.5%) and about 62% of genera died out in the terminal Permian event.

perspectives.holder: Earlier rarefaction estimates (Raup 1979; Sepkoski 1986), still widely quoted, e.g. by MIT News in 2015
perspectives.account: Roughly 88–96% of marine species were lost; Stanley argues these figures merged the Guadalupian and end-Permian crises, which were not recognised as separate until 1994.

perspectives.holder: Gastaldo et al. (2020), Nature Communications
perspectives.account: The base of the Lystrosaurus Assemblage Zone in the Karoo Basin dates to 252.24 ± 0.11 Ma, so the classic terrestrial vertebrate turnover there preceded the marine extinction by over 300,000 years and may have had different causes.

perspectives.holder: Ward et al. (2005); Smith and Botha-Brink (2014), as summarised by Gastaldo et al. (2020)
perspectives.account: Carbon-isotope and magnetic-polarity correlations place the Karoo vertebrate turnover at the same time as the marine crisis, making land and sea losses one event.

perspectives.holder: Burgess and Bowring (2015); Burgess, Muirhead and Bowring (2017)
perspectives.account: Siberian Traps magmatism is a plausible trigger; the extinction coincides with the onset of sill intrusion and contact metamorphism of basin sediments rather than with the earlier lava floods. MIT reported the authors still treat the link as plausible rather than proven.

records.title: Emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa
records.summary: Around 300,000 years ago our species, Homo sapiens, was taking shape in Africa. The oldest fossils of its lineage, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are dated to about 315,000 years ago and pair a modern-looking face with an older, elongated braincase.
records.card: Fossils, stone tools and genomes all place the origin of Homo sapiens in Africa during the Middle Pleistocene. Jebel Irhoud in Morocco (about 315,000 years ago), Florisbad in South Africa (about 259,000, disputed) and Omo Kibish in Ethiopia (at least 233,000) show the species' features appearing across the continent. Many researchers now think it arose from several linked populations rather than in one cradle.
records.what:
Homo sapiens, the species to which every living person belongs, evolved in Africa from earlier Middle Pleistocene humans, often grouped as Homo heidelbergensis or Homo rhodesiensis. Its emergence was a gradual process rather than a single event, and the fossil record of it is thin.

The oldest fossils now assigned to the H. sapiens lineage come from Jebel Irhoud, a karst cave in a limestone massif southeast of Safi, Morocco. Mining exposed the site in the early 1960s, and a nearly complete skull was found by accident. Excavations led by Jean-Jacques Hublin (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology) and Abdelouahed Ben-Ncer (INSAP, Rabat) from 2004 raised the number of hominin fossils from 6 to 22, representing at least five individuals: three adults, an adolescent and a child of about eight. Thermoluminescence dating of burnt flint tools from the same layer gave a weighted average of 315,000 ± 34,000 years, and a re-dated tooth from the 1960s Irhoud 3 jaw gave 286,000 ± 32,000 years. Earlier estimates had put the fossils at about 40,000 and later 160,000 years, and had read them as an African Neanderthal or a late archaic group.

The Irhoud people had faces and teeth that fall within the range of living humans, but their braincases were long and low rather than globular. Their tools were Middle Stone Age Levallois flakes and points, and they hunted mainly gazelle.

Other early fossils lie far away. A partial skull from Florisbad, South Africa, has an ESR date of 259,000 ± 35,000 years on an associated tooth, although whether the tooth and skull belong together is disputed. Omo I from the Kibish Formation in southern Ethiopia, found in 1967 and long dated to about 195,000 years, is at least 233,000 ± 22,000 years old. Herto, also in Ethiopia, dates to about 160,000–155,000 years ago.

Researchers disagree on how to read this spread: some see a pan-African process among loosely connected populations, while others stress that Irhoud is only an early, partly archaic member of the lineage.

uncertainty.note: Start: thermoluminescence weighted average for Jebel Irhoud layer 7, 315 ± 34 ka at 1 sigma; the 95% range is 383–247 ka (Richter et al. 2017). End: the minimum age of Omo I, 233 ± 22 ka at 2 sigma (Vidal et al. 2022), chosen as the earliest dated fossil with fully modern cranial features; it is a minimum, and Hublin et al. argue braincase shape kept evolving within H. sapiens after this. Genetic estimates of the deepest population split range from 350–260 ka (Schlebusch et al. 2017) to 135–120 ka among present-day populations (Ragsdale et al. 2023), depending on the model. The process has no sharp start or end.

records.how: No single event made Homo sapiens. Three lines of evidence show how it happened. First, the fossils show a mosaic. At Jebel Irhoud the face, jaw and teeth were already within modern human variation by about 315,000 years ago, while the braincase stayed long and low. Hublin and colleagues infer that the face was established early and that later evolution mainly reshaped the brain and braincase, probably through genetic changes affecting brain organisation and development. Second, the tools. Levallois-based Middle Stone Age assemblages appear by about 300,000 years ago at Jebel Irhoud and Olorgesailie, before 275,000–285,000 years ago at Gademotta and in the Kapthurin Formation, and about 280,000 years ago at Florisbad. Richter and colleagues suggest the species and the technology emerged close together in time, possibly across the continent. Third, the environment and population structure. Middle Pleistocene green Sahara episodes, one especially marked around 330,000 years ago, shrank the desert and allowed ecological contact between north and sub-Saharan Africa. Scerri and colleagues argue that shifting habitats split early humans into subdivided populations linked by occasional gene flow, so modern traits appeared piecemeal in different places. Genetic models differ on the details: Schlebusch and colleagues put the deepest split among modern human populations at 350,000–260,000 years ago, while Ragsdale and colleagues model two or more weakly differentiated stem populations exchanging migrants, with the earliest divergence among living populations 120,000–135,000 years ago. Dating relies on thermoluminescence of burnt flint, ESR and U-series on teeth, and argon–argon dating of volcanic ash.
records.why_it_matters: Every person alive today belongs to the species whose beginnings these fossils record, and every later chapter of human history follows from it, from the dispersals out of Africa to the peopling of every continent. The 2017 Jebel Irhoud dates changed how that beginning is understood. Before them, most researchers placed a single cradle in East Africa about 200,000 years ago, based on Omo Kibish and Herto. The Moroccan fossils pushed the lineage back by roughly 100,000 years and put North Africa, long overlooked, at the centre of the debate. Together with Florisbad, the re-dating of Omo I to at least 233,000 years ago and new genetic models, this has shifted many researchers toward a picture of several linked African populations, with no single birthplace. That shift has a practical consequence for science: geneticists now test models with population structure and gene flow, and published split times now differ by more than 100,000 years depending on the model. Dating matters to the counterfactual too. Had Jebel Irhoud kept its earlier ages of about 40,000 or 160,000 years, its fossils would still be read as an African Neanderthal or a late archaic survivor, and the East African cradle model would face no North African challenge. Richter and colleagues also link the green Sahara episodes to continuity between the Maghreb and the rest of Africa. On that reasoning, without such humid windows the populations north and south of the desert would have been more isolated, and a continent-wide process would have been harder to sustain.

related.because: The African Homo sapiens populations that formed from about 300,000 years ago were the source of the much later dispersals that carried the species beyond Africa.

perspectives.account: Jebel Irhoud, at about 315,000 years ago, documents an early stage of the H. sapiens clade, and with Florisbad shows the species' emergence involved the whole African continent, not sub-Saharan Africa alone. perspectives.account: The Irhoud people are probable early members of the H. sapiens lineage with a mix of archaic and modern traits, not fully modern humans. Several early H. sapiens populations probably lived in different parts of Africa around 300,000 years ago, alongside other lineages such as H. naledi.

perspectives.holder: Scerri et al. (2018), 22 authors, Trends in Ecology & Evolution
perspectives.account: H. sapiens evolved within a set of subdivided, interlinked populations across Africa whose connections shifted with climate, so derived traits appeared in a mosaic. They call this African multiregionalism and reject a single panmictic origin.

perspectives.holder: Schlebusch et al. (2017), Science; Ragsdale et al. (2023), Nature
perspectives.account: Genomes give different split times depending on the model. Schlebusch's team places the deepest divergence among modern humans at 350,000–260,000 years ago. Ragsdale's team finds that two or more weakly differentiated stem populations linked by gene flow fit better than a single origin or archaic admixture, with present-day structure dating only to 120,000–135,000 years ago.

perspectives.account: The 259,000-year ESR date comes from a tooth that may not belong with the Florisbad skull, and the spring deposits were disturbed, so current data do not show H. sapiens in southern Africa at about 260,000 years ago.

records.title: Invention of writing
records.summary: Writing, the recording of a language in visible signs, was invented independently at least four times: in southern Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3300–3100 BCE, in Shang China by about 1200 BCE, and in Mesoamerica during the first millennium BCE.
records.card: The oldest known writing comes from Uruk in southern Iraq, where temple administrators listed goods and labour on clay tablets around 3200 BCE, and from Tomb U-j at Abydos in Egypt, radiocarbon-dated to about 3320 BCE. Diviners at the Shang court in Anyang were using a mature Chinese script on bone and shell by about 1220 BCE, and Mesoamerican scripts appear by the middle of the first millennium BCE. Most scholars now count these as separate inventions, but which came first, and whether clay counting tokens gave rise to cuneiform, are still argued.
records.what:
Writing is a system of visible marks that records a particular language, as distinct from pictures, tallies or emblems that convey meaning without fixing words. The Oriental Institute's survey Visible Language (Woods, ed., 2010) identifies four 'pristine' inventions, made without any exposure to an existing script: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. Other scripts are thought likely to derive from, or to have been inspired by, these four.

In Mesopotamia the earliest tablets come from the Eanna temple precinct at Uruk, a city of perhaps 20,000–50,000 people covering about 2.5 km² in the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE). The German Archaeological Institute excavated about five thousand proto-cuneiform tablets there between 1928 and 1976, and the whole corpus now numbers roughly six thousand tablets and fragments. Because they were found discarded in rubbish fill, their dates are approximate: the earlier script phase, Uruk IV, is conventionally placed about 3200 BCE and the later Uruk III phase about 3100 BCE, while a single charcoal sample points to 3500–3390 BCE. Almost all are administrative records of goods, rations and labour.

In Egypt, Günter Dreyer's re-excavation of Tomb U-j in the royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa'ab at Abydos recovered nearly 200 incised bone and ivory tags and 125 ink inscriptions on pottery, dated by radiocarbon to about 3320 BCE. The signs mainly record names of places, institutions and rulers, and some already use the rebus principle.

In China, the earliest certain writing is the oracle-bone inscriptions from Anyang, records of royal divinations made under the last nine Shang kings (c. 1220–1050 BCE). In Mesoamerica, Olmec and Zapotec scripts preceded Maya writing; a carved monument at San José Mogote in Oaxaca is dated to about 600 BCE, and the earliest known Maya text, at San Bartolo in Guatemala, to 300–200 BCE. Early Mesoamerican scripts remain largely undeciphered.

Scholars still disagree about which invention came first, because the Abydos radiocarbon dates have been questioned and the Uruk tablets cannot be closely dated, and about whether Mesopotamian clay tokens were the direct ancestors of cuneiform signs.

uncertainty.note: Start: Tomb U-j at Abydos, c. 3320 BCE by calibrated radiocarbon (Boehmer, Dreyer and Kromer 1993, as cited in Visible Language), a dating others have questioned (Hendrickx 2006); Bayesian modelling puts the Naqada IID/IIIA transition, when Egyptian writing first appears, at 3377–3238 BCE (95%). Uruk IV is conventionally c. 3200 BCE; a lone charcoal sample from tablet contexts gives 3500–3390 BCE. End: the Mesoamerican invention is placed in the Early or Middle Formative (c. 1200–600 BCE); the earliest dated inscriptions are at San José Mogote (c. 600 BCE) and San Bartolo (300–200 BCE). China's earliest certain writing (c. 1220–1050 BCE) falls between these bounds.

records.how:
In Mesopotamia writing grew out of administration. Uruk's rapid growth in the later fourth millennium BCE created institutions that had to track rations, livestock, materials and labour. Before writing, accountants used small clay tokens, some sealed inside hollow clay envelopes whose outer surface could be impressed with the tokens inside, an interpretation first proposed by Pierre Amiet in the 1960s; then came numerical tablets carrying only number signs, and finally tablets that added one or two signs naming the commodity. Some proto-cuneiform numerals were made by pressing tokens into the clay, but most word signs were new pictographs, with a few borrowed from token shapes and from temple emblems such as Inana's symbol. Uruk IV signs were drawn with a pointed stylus; in the Uruk III phase about a century later their lines were straightened and impressed with a stylus of triangular cross-section, the beginning of wedge-shaped cuneiform. The system soon reached Jemdet Nasr, Khafajah and Tell Uqair, and possibly inspired proto-Elamite writing in Iran about 3100 BCE.

All four pristine systems started from logograms, signs for whole words, extended them with the rebus principle (using a sign for its sound to write a different word), and developed semantic determinatives. The Abydos tags already spell the town of Elephantine with an elephant over a hill sign. The settings differed: accounting at Uruk; labelling of goods and naming of elites, then royal display, in Egypt; divination on turtle shell and ox bone at the Shang court; and largely commemorative, calendrical texts in Mesoamerica. Some scholars argue that administrative records also existed in the latter cases on perishable papyrus, bamboo or bark. In every early state literacy was confined to a tiny elite, estimated at under 1 per cent of the population.
records.why_it_matters: Writing gave the first states a memory that outlasted any single official. Uruk's administrators could keep account of rations, labour and herds across years, and the technique spread across Babylonia within about a century and was later adapted to write unrelated languages, among them Akkadian, Elamite and Hittite. Over the following centuries writing moved beyond bookkeeping: in Mesopotamia letters, religious and historical texts appear only from the middle of the third millennium BCE, some seven hundred years after the first tablets. Writing also divides the human past into the documented and the undocumented, since from these points on rulers, places, prices and beliefs survive in their own terms, not only as objects in the ground. The Chinese script that descends from the Shang oracle-bone inscriptions is the only one of the four pristine systems still in use, so a continuous line of development runs from the Anyang diviners to Chinese writing today. The separate inventions matter as well: they show that writing was not a single lucky discovery that spread from Sumer, as scholars assumed in the mid-twentieth century, but something several societies arrived at for different reasons, from accounting to display, divination and commemoration. Without writing, early administrations would have depended on tokens, seals and the memory of officials, and knowledge of the ancient world would rest on archaeology alone. Because early literacy was confined to a small elite, the first written records also speak far more for temples and courts than for the farmers and workers they counted.

perspectives.holder: Ignace J. Gelb (A Study of Writing, 1952) and earlier proponents of monogenesis, as summarised by Woods (2010)
perspectives.account: Writing was invented only once, by the Sumerians; the idea, not the technology, then spread by 'stimulus diffusion' to Egypt and eventually China, while New World scripts were not true writing.

perspectives.holder: Christopher Woods and contributors to Visible Language (2010), reflecting current majority scholarship
perspectives.account: There were at least four independent, 'pristine' inventions (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica). Maya decipherment proved New World writing genuine, the Abydos finds made Egyptian writing as old as Mesopotamian, and the Chinese system is too different and too distant to derive from cuneiform.

perspectives.holder: Excavators of Tomb U-j (Dreyer and colleagues) and the Visible Language Egypt chapters; supported in broad terms by Dee et al. (2013)
perspectives.account: Egyptian writing at Abydos dates to about 3320 BCE by radiocarbon, at least as early as proto-cuneiform; Dee et al. find that Naqada IIIA, when writing first appears in Egypt, coincides closely with the first cuneiform.

perspectives.holder: Hendrickx (2006), as cited in Visible Language
perspectives.account: The calibrated radiocarbon dates for Tomb U-j are open to question, so Egyptian priority over Mesopotamia is not established; relative Naqada-period dating remains the preferred framework.

perspectives.holder: Andréas Stauder (2010)
perspectives.account: Egyptian writing can be modelled as a local development rooted in emblematic display, against the long-controversial hypothesis of Mesopotamian influence; its near-simultaneous emergence with cuneiform reflects related political and economic changes across the late fourth-millennium Near East.

perspectives.holder: Denise Schmandt-Besserat (1992 onward)
perspectives.account: Cuneiform evolved directly from a token accounting system: plain tokens from about 7500 BCE became numerals, complex tokens of the fourth millennium became word signs, and impressed envelopes (c. 3300 BCE) were the bridge to tablets.

perspectives.holder: Critics including Paul Zimansky (1993) and Christopher Woods (2010)
perspectives.account: Only the numeral signs clearly relate to token impressions; many proposed token-to-sign matches are implausible, and the token record is too scattered across millennia to be one uniform system.

perspectives.holder: Saturno, Stuart and Beltrán (2006), as reported by Mesoweb
perspectives.account: San Bartolo shows the Maya were writing by 300–200 BCE, nearly as early as any Mesoamerican script, and Maya writing may have influenced the Isthmian script rather than the reverse; Palka (2010) instead sees Maya writing as adopted from Olmec or Zapotec neighbours.

records.title: Origin of life
records.summary: Life on Earth arose from non-living chemistry at an unknown time between about 4.5 and 3.5 billion years ago; the oldest evidence most scientists accept is 3.43–3.48-billion-year-old microbial structures in Western Australia's Pilbara.
records.card: No one knows exactly when or where living cells first appeared, but the window is bounded by the Moon-forming impact about 4.5 billion years ago and by fossil microbial mats in the Pilbara of Western Australia about 3.48 to 3.43 billion years old. Older claims from Greenland, Quebec and a single Australian zircon, reaching back to 4.1 billion years, remain disputed. Gene-based molecular clocks place the common ancestor of all living things near 4.2 billion years ago, which would push the origin earlier still.
records.what:
The origin of life is the transition, sometime in Earth's first billion years, from prebiotic chemistry to self-sustaining, evolving cells. It left no direct record, so its timing is bracketed by indirect evidence. The upper limit is set by the giant impact that formed the Moon about 4.51 billion years ago, which would have sterilized the young planet. The lower limit comes from the oldest traces of life that most researchers accept. In the Strelley Pool Chert of the Pilbara Craton, Western Australia, a fossil reef roughly 3.43 billion years old contains seven distinct stromatolite forms whose variety and links to their environment point to microbial builders. The slightly older Dresser Formation nearby, about 3.48 billion years old, preserves stromatolites, organic matter and hot-spring deposits that suggest microbes lived even on land.

Older claims are vigorously disputed. In 2016 a team described 1–4 cm cone-shaped stromatolites in 3.7-billion-year-old rocks at Isua, southwest Greenland; in 2018 another team argued from three-dimensional shape, orientation and chemistry that they are deformation features formed after burial. Haematite tubes and filaments in vent rocks of the Nuvvuagittuq belt, Quebec, at least 3.77 and possibly 4.28 billion years old, have been interpreted as microfossils, though their authors concede abiotic mineral growth cannot be fully excluded and the belt's age is itself debated. Graphite with an isotopically light, life-like carbon signature sits sealed inside a 4.10-billion-year-old zircon from the Jack Hills, Western Australia, but it is one grain and non-biological origins are possible. Independently, molecular-clock studies of gene families date the last universal common ancestor of all cells to about 4.2 billion years ago (4.09–4.33), implying an origin within a few hundred million years of the Moon-forming impact. Sources therefore disagree by more than 600 million years on when life is first securely recorded, because they weigh ambiguous chemical and structural traces differently. Where it began is equally open: submarine hydrothermal vents and volcanic hot springs on land are the two leading candidate settings.

uncertainty.note: This is a window, not a dated event. Start = the Moon-forming impact (~4,510 Ma), used by Moody et al. (2024) as the maximum age for life; the actual origin could fall anywhere after it. End = the oldest evidence of life most researchers accept: Dresser Formation c. 3,480 Ma, or Strelley Pool c. 3,430 Ma if only that reef is accepted (end_plus 50 Myr). If disputed claims are accepted, life is recorded earlier: Isua ~3,700 Ma, Nuvvuagittuq ≥3,770 Ma (possibly 4,280 Ma), Jack Hills graphite 4,100 Ma (end_minus 620 Myr). The record id keeps the queue's -3700my label, which corresponds to the contested Isua claim, not to a consensus date.
