records.how: The steps from chemistry to cells are not directly preserved and remain hypotheses tested in laboratories. In one family of scenarios, life began at alkaline hydrothermal vents on the sea floor, where mineral surfaces and chemical gradients could drive carbon fixation; the inferred metabolism of the last universal common ancestor, an anaerobe using the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway to fix carbon, is consistent with a hydrogen-rich setting of this kind. A rival scenario places it in volcanic hot-spring pools on land, where repeated wetting and drying concentrates organic monomers, links them into polymers, and wraps them in lipid membranes as protocells; the 3.48-billion-year-old Dresser Formation hot-spring deposits are cited as a plausible ancient example. Either way, the sequence must have produced self-replicating molecules, membranes and energy metabolism, and then a population of cells from which all modern life descends. Evidence for the result is read in three ways: fossil structures such as stromatolites built by microbial mats; microfossil-like filaments; and carbon depleted in carbon-13, a signature of enzymatic carbon fixation that can, however, also arise without life. Ancient rocks are metamorphosed and deformed, which is why claims older than about 3.5 billion years are hard to confirm.
records.why_it_matters: Every organism that has ever lived, from the first microbial mats to the Cambrian animals, dinosaurs and humans, descends from the cells that emerged in this process, so it is the precondition for every other record in the life and human layers of the Atlas. Its direct consequences reshaped the planet itself: by about 3.4 billion years ago microbial communities were building reefs across a shallow carbonate platform, and their descendants went on to evolve oxygen-producing photosynthesis, which transformed the atmosphere and oceans. Had life not arisen, Earth's surface chemistry would have been governed by geology alone, with no oxygen-rich air, no biologically built limestones or soils, and no fossil fuels. The question of how early life appeared also matters beyond Earth. If molecular clocks are right that a complex common ancestor already existed about 4.2 billion years ago, life arose within a few hundred million years of the planet becoming habitable, which suggests that it may emerge readily wherever conditions allow. If instead only the Pilbara evidence stands, the window is longer and the case for quick emergence weaker. That uncertainty shapes the search for life on Mars: the Pilbara and Isua debates are used by NASA and others as test cases for telling genuine biosignatures from mineral look-alikes in rocks of similar age, including the samples collected by the Perseverance rover in Jezero Crater.

related.because: Earth's accretion and the cooling of its surface after the Moon-forming impact produced the oceans, rock surfaces and chemical gradients in which life could arise.
The Cambrian animal radiation was built on about three billion years of evolution by descendants of the first cells, which supplied the genetic and metabolic toolkit animals inherited.

perspectives.holder: Conservative reading of the rock record (e.g. Allwood et al. 2006; Djokic et al. 2017; Duda et al. 2016)
perspectives.account: The oldest evidence that withstands scrutiny is in the Pilbara Craton: the c. 3.43 Ga Strelley Pool stromatolite reef, whose seven forms and environmental patterns argue for microbial builders, and the c. 3.48 Ga Dresser Formation with stromatolites, organic matter and hot-spring textures. Life was certainly present by about 3.5 Ga.

perspectives.holder: Nutman, Bennett, Friend, Van Kranendonk and colleagues (2016)
perspectives.account: Conical and domical structures 1–4 cm high in 3.7 Ga Isua metacarbonates are stromatolites formed in shallow seawater, pushing the fossil record back about 220 million years and implying that life emerged rapidly, in the Hadean.

perspectives.holder: Allwood, Rosing and colleagues (2018)
perspectives.account: Three-dimensional shape, orientation relative to the rock fabric, and element chemistry show the Isua structures are deformation features formed long after burial, not stromatolites; the case is a caution for life detection on Mars.

perspectives.holder: Dodd, Papineau and colleagues (2017, 2022)
perspectives.account: Haematite tubes and filaments in Nuvvuagittuq vent-related jasper, at least 3.77 and possibly 4.28 Ga, are best explained as remains of iron-oxidizing microbes, though the authors concede abiotic chemical gardens cannot be fully excluded. The belt's maximum age is itself disputed: the Québec lexicon treats a 4,321 Ma Sm-Nd age as controversial, against U-Pb zircon ages near 3.78–3.82 Ga.

perspectives.holder: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison and Mao (2015), with commentary by House (2015)
perspectives.account: Graphite sealed in a 4.10 Ga Jack Hills zircon has a carbon-13-depleted signature (−24 ± 5‰) consistent with biology, so a biosphere may have existed 300 million years earlier than thought; the commentary stresses that it is a single grain and that a non-biological, isotopically light carbon source cannot be ruled out.

perspectives.holder: Molecular-clock phylogenetics (Moody et al. 2024)
perspectives.account: Dating ancient gene duplications places the last universal common ancestor at about 4.2 Ga (4.09–4.33), already an anaerobic acetogen whose genome encoded roughly 2,600 proteins, living in an established ecosystem, so life's origin must have followed the Moon-forming impact within a few hundred million years. These are model estimates sensitive to calibration.

perspectives.holder: Setting debate: land hot springs (Damer & Deamer 2020) versus submarine hydrothermal vents
perspectives.account: Hot-spring advocates argue that wet-dry cycling in freshwater volcanic pools concentrates and polymerizes organic molecules and that seawater hinders membrane assembly; vent advocates place origins at alkaline sea-floor vents with natural chemical gradients. Neither is established.

records.title: Extinction of the Neanderthals
records.summary: Neanderthals, the archaic humans of Europe and western and central Asia, vanished from the archaeological record by about 41,000–39,000 years ago, after a few thousand years of overlap with incoming Homo sapiens; part of their DNA survives in people outside Africa.
records.card: Radiocarbon dating of 40 sites from Spain to Russia places the end of the Neanderthal-made Mousterian stone industry at 41,030–39,260 calibrated years before present, with populations disappearing region by region rather than all at once. Neanderthals and modern humans shared Europe for roughly 2,600–5,400 years and interbred, so about 1.5–2.1% of the genome of people outside Africa is Neanderthal-derived. Claims of later survival in southern Iberia are still disputed, and the cause is debated between climate stress, small populations, competition and assimilation.
records.what:
Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) lived across Europe and southwestern to central Asia from about 400,000 until about 40,000 years ago, according to the Smithsonian's Human Origins Program. They made Mousterian tools struck from prepared stone cores, controlled fire, made clothing and buried some of their dead. Their extinction is dated chiefly by the last Mousterian layers and the last Neanderthal fossils.

The most widely cited chronology is that of Higham and colleagues (2014), who dated about 200 samples of bone, charcoal and shell from 40 sites between Spain and Russia with improved accelerator radiocarbon methods, including ultrafiltration of bone collagen to remove younger contaminating carbon. Their Bayesian model places the end of the Mousterian across Europe at 41,030–39,260 calibrated years before present (cal BP, counted back from 1950 CE) at 95.4% probability. The Châtelperronian, a so-called transitional industry often attributed to Neanderthals, ended at about the same time. The disappearance was staggered: the authors describe a mosaic in which Neanderthal and modern human groups occupied different parts of Europe for 2,600–5,400 years.

The two populations interbred. The draft Neanderthal genome (Green et al. 2010), built from three bones from Vindija Cave in Croatia plus smaller samples from Spain, Germany and Russia, showed that Neanderthals share more genetic variants with non-Africans than with Africans, and the high-coverage genome from Denisova Cave in the Altai (Prüfer et al. 2014) put the Neanderthal-derived share of non-African genomes at about 1.5–2.1%.

The end date is disputed at the margins. Finlayson and colleagues (2006) argued that Neanderthals survived at Gorham's Cave, Gibraltar, until about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago, and Zilhão and colleagues (2017) argue that the Mousterian lasted south of the Ebro valley until about 37,000 years ago; Wood and colleagues (2013) and Higham's team found the southern Iberian late dates unreliable. Why Neanderthals disappeared is also unresolved: climate stress, small and inbred populations, competition with modern humans and absorption into their populations all have advocates.

uncertainty.note: Start is the beginning of overlap with Homo sapiens in Europe, c. 45,000 cal BP (early Uluzzian dates reported in the 2014 Oxford/Tübingen release); combining Higham et al.'s 2,600–5,400-year overlap with their end date implies an overlap start of roughly 46,430–41,860 cal BP, which sets the start range. End is the midpoint of the 95.4% range for the end of the Mousterian, 41,030–39,260 cal BP (Higham et al. 2014). Conversions use year = 1950 − cal BP. Disputed later survival is not included in the range: southern Iberian Mousterian to c. 37,100–36,500 years ago (Zilhão et al. 2017, year ≈ −35,150 to −34,550) and Gorham's Cave to c. 28,000 radiocarbon (uncalibrated) years BP (Finlayson et al. 2006).

records.how: No single mechanism is agreed, but the sequence is fairly clear. (1) Modern humans reached Europe while Neanderthals still lived there: the Uluzzian of Italy, which Higham's team associates with the earliest dated modern humans in Europe, has early dates of about 45,000 years ago. (2) Stalagmites from Ascunsă and Tăușoare caves in the Romanian Carpathians record two severe cold, dry stadials, Greenland Stadial 12 (about 44.3–43.3 ka) and Greenland Stadial 10 (about 40.8–40.2 ka). Near-sterile archaeological layers in the Danube basin and across the Châtelperronian area coincide with them, and Staubwasser and colleagues argue that spreading steppe emptied Neanderthal territories region by region, which modern humans, who seem to have been better adapted to steppe, then reoccupied. (3) Neanderthal numbers were already small: genetic estimates cited by Vaesen and colleagues put their effective population at no more than about 3,000–3,900 over their last 400,000 years, and the Altai Neanderthal's parents were related about as closely as half-siblings. (4) Population models show that groups this small can die out within 10,000 years through reproduction-related Allee effects, inbreeding and chance fluctuations, even without competitors; modern humans may have hastened this by fragmenting Neanderthal ranges. (5) Interbreeding moved Neanderthal DNA into modern human populations, and Villa and Roebroeks argue that low density, gene flow and a shrinking range ended in genetic swamping and assimilation. (6) By 41,030–39,260 cal BP the Mousterian had ended across Europe, with any later survival in southern Iberia still disputed.
records.why_it_matters: The Neanderthals' disappearance left Homo sapiens as the only human population in Europe, after Neanderthals had lived there and in western and central Asia for some 360,000 years. It was not a clean break. Because the two populations met and interbred, about 1.5–2.1% of the genome of everyone with non-African ancestry today is Neanderthal-derived, and Denisovans in the Altai also carried Neanderthal DNA; that inheritance is a direct, measurable consequence of the contact that preceded the extinction. The event also changed how scholars think about human uniqueness. Villa and Roebroeks found no archaeologically visible inferiority in Neanderthal technology, subsistence or social life, and UNESCO cites Gorham's Cave engravings older than 39,000 years as evidence of Neanderthal abstract thought, so the extinction can no longer be told simply as superior newcomers replacing inferior natives. Dating it drove a methodological shift as well: ultrafiltration showed that many young radiocarbon dates were contaminated, rewriting chronologies of the Middle-to-Upper Palaeolithic transition from Iberia to Russia. Had Neanderthals survived, people outside Africa might today share the planet with a second kind of human instead of carrying fragments of its genome; yet Vaesen's models suggest that, being so few, they might have vanished even if modern humans had never arrived.

related.because: The dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa brought modern humans into Neanderthal territory, creating the overlap, interbreeding and possible competition or range fragmentation that most explanations of the extinction invoke.

perspectives.holder: Higham et al. (2014), Nature; University of Oxford-led team
perspectives.account: With ultrafiltered radiocarbon dates from 40 sites, the Mousterian ends across Europe at 41,030–39,260 cal BP, at different times in different regions, after a 2,600–5,400-year overlap with modern humans. The team could not confirm proposed later refuges in Iberia or at Gorham's Cave and attributes many younger dates to contamination.

perspectives.holder: Finlayson, Giles Pacheco, Rodríguez-Vidal et al. (2006), Nature; Gibraltar Museum
perspectives.account: Hearth charcoal dates from Gorham's Cave show Neanderthals surviving there until about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago, long after modern humans arrived, in isolated southern refuges.

perspectives.holder: Zilhão and Pettitt (2006), Before Farming; Paul Mellars as reported by Nature News
perspectives.account: The Gorham's samples are microscopic, scattered and not ordered by depth; the young dates more likely belong to Upper Palaeolithic use of the cave, and Middle Palaeolithic occupation lasted to about 32,000–30,000 radiocarbon years ago but not later. Mellars warned that small amounts of contamination make dates too young.

perspectives.holder: Zilhão et al. (2017), Heliyon (the Ebro Frontier model)
perspectives.account: In Murcia the Mousterian ends no earlier than about 37,100 years ago and the Aurignacian begins by about 36,500, so Neanderthals persisted south of the Ebro at least 3,000 years after their disappearance elsewhere, behind a biogeographical barrier.

perspectives.holder: Wood et al. (2013), PNAS
perspectives.account: Of 11 southern Iberian sites tested, only Jarama VI and Zafarraya yielded datable bone, and both gave ages at least 10,000 radiocarbon years older than before; late Neanderthal survival in the south rests on at most one possible site, Cueva Antón.

perspectives.holder: Staubwasser et al. (2018), PNAS (climate-driven depopulation)
perspectives.account: Cold, arid stadials GS12 and GS10 expanded steppe and emptied Neanderthal regions at different times, letting better-adapted modern humans repopulate them; the authors note causality is not fully demonstrated.

perspectives.holder: Vaesen, Scherjon, Hemerik and Verpoorte (2019), PLOS ONE (small-population null model)
perspectives.account: Inbreeding, reproduction-related Allee effects and random demographic swings could have extinguished Neanderthal populations of 50 to 5,000 within 10,000 years without competition or climate change; any role of modern humans was probably indirect.

perspectives.holder: Villa and Roebroeks (2014), PLOS ONE (assimilation)
perspectives.account: The archaeological record shows no Neanderthal inferiority in weapons, subsistence or social organisation; disappearance was a protracted process of low density, interbreeding and a shrinking range ending in genetic swamping, though interbreeding may have been too limited for full assimilation.

perspectives.holder: Smithsonian Human Origins Program; competition models summarised by Vaesen et al. (2019)
perspectives.account: Modern humans spreading into Europe during a cold period may have prevented Neanderthals from re-expanding into favoured areas, and many scholars propose that modern humans out-competed them for resources; whether climate or competition mattered more remains open.

records.title: Formation of Earth
records.summary: About 4.54 billion years ago, give or take roughly one percent, dust, rock and planetary embryos orbiting the young Sun collided and merged into the Earth; a last giant impact probably made the Moon.
records.card: Earth was assembled over tens of millions of years from planetesimals and Moon- to Mars-sized embryos left over from the Sun's birth. Lead isotopes in meteorites and ancient ores put the planet's age at 4.54 billion years, an answer first reached by Clair Patterson in the 1950s. Zircon grains from Western Australia show that a crust and probably liquid water existed by 4.4 billion years ago.
records.what:
Earth formed by accretion: in the disk of gas and dust around the newborn Sun, grains clumped into planetesimals tens of kilometres across, these grew into planetary embryos roughly the size of the Moon or Mars, and the embryos in the inner Solar System then collided with one another until a few rocky planets remained. Meteorite solids give the starting point of this sequence; the International Commission on Stratigraphy places the base of the informal Hadean Eon at 4,567 million years ago.

The age usually quoted for the Earth itself is 4.54 billion years, with an uncertainty of less than one percent according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It rests on lead isotopes: comparing the ratio of lead-207 to lead-206 in the oldest terrestrial lead ores with that in uranium-free minerals of iron meteorites such as Canyon Diablo. Clair Patterson of the California Institute of Technology calculated about 4.55 billion years in 1953 and published 4.55 ± 0.07 billion years in 1956; Tera's 1980 analysis of four ancient lead deposits gave the 4.54 figure now in common use. Earth's own oldest materials are younger, because plate tectonics has recycled the first crust: rocks of the Acasta Gneiss in Canada reach about 4.03 billion years, and a detrital zircon from the Jack Hills of Western Australia has been dated to 4,404 ± 8 million years.

The final large collision in Earth's growth is thought to have produced the Moon. This giant-impact hypothesis is the leading explanation, but its details are debated: whether the impactor, called Theia, was a single Mars-sized body or something else, how energetic the collision was, whether the Moon formed slowly from a debris disk or almost at once, and when it happened, with estimates from about 40 to 150 million years after the first meteorite solids. Scholars also note that it is not settled whether the 4.54 billion-year age records accretion itself, the separation of the core, or the material Earth was built from.

No continents existed during this interval, so the globe shows the whole planet without a map.

uncertainty.note: Start is the conventional age of Earth, 4.54 Ga with < 1% uncertainty (USGS; Tera 1980 via Dalrymple 2001); the minus bound reaches 4.567 Ga, the age of the first meteorite solids and base of the Hadean (ICS 2024/12), when accretion began. End is the Moon-forming impact, commonly given as about 4.5 Ga (NASA: ~60 Myr after the Solar System began); Hf-W estimates span 40-150 Myr after the first solids, i.e. about 4.527-4.417 Ga (Raymond 2024, citing Kleine and Walker 2017). Dalrymple (2001) notes it is unresolved whether 4.54 Ga dates accretion, core formation or Earth's source material.

records.how: The process ran in stages. Dust in the Sun's protoplanetary disk clumped into planetesimals about 10 to 100 km across, which grew by collisions (and possibly by sweeping up drifting pebbles) into planetary embryos of roughly 0.01 to 0.1 Earth masses. After the disk's gas dispersed, the rocky planets finished growing through a series of giant impacts between embryos. The heat of these impacts melted Earth, letting iron and iron-loving elements sink to form the core; the hafnium-182 to tungsten-182 decay system (half-life about 9 million years) records when this separation happened. The last giant impact, probably the Moon-forming one, ended the main growth phase. Afterwards, during so-called late accretion, smaller planetesimals added only about half a percent of Earth's mass. The planet's age is read from lead isotopes: uranium decays to lead at known rates, so the lead-207/lead-206 ratio in ancient terrestrial ores, compared with nearly uranium-free troilite in iron meteorites such as Canyon Diablo, fixes a common starting age for Earth and meteorites.
records.why_it_matters:
This is the opening event of everything else in the Atlas: every rock, ocean, organism and human story on the globe happened on the planet assembled here. Its outcome set conditions that still govern Earth. The giant impacts melted the planet and let iron sink into a core, separating it from the rocky mantle; the probable Moon-forming collision gave Earth a large satellite whose gravity is the main cause of ocean tides, and whose slow retreat from Earth is still lengthening the day. Within about 150 million years, zircons from Western Australia show, there was continental-type crust and probably liquid water, the setting in which life later began. If the final collisions had been different, Earth might have had no large Moon, a different mass or a different spin, and the history recorded on this globe would not have followed the same course.

The measurement matters too. Patterson’s 1956 meteorite-lead age settled a question on which early twentieth-century estimates had ranged from a few million to billions of years, and gave geology and biology a firm span of time within which evolution and plate tectonics had to fit. His later work to remove human-made lead from the environment, especially from petrol, grew out of the same laboratory methods. Today the 4.54 billion-year figure anchors the geologic time scale used by Earth scientists, and the Atlas’s own time axis begins at it.

perspectives.holder: Canonical giant-impact model (leading view; e.g. Canup and colleagues, summarised by Raymond 2024 and NASA)
perspectives.account: A Mars-mass embryo, Theia, struck an Earth that had about 90 percent of its present mass, and the Moon gathered from the debris disk. It explains the Moon's orbit, but predicts a Moon made mostly of impactor material, which conflicts with the near-identical oxygen isotopes of Earth and Moon unless Theia formed very close to Earth.

perspectives.holder: High-energy impact variants, including the synestia hypothesis
perspectives.account: A faster-spinning proto-Earth, an impact between two roughly equal embryos, or a collision so energetic that it made a doughnut of rock vapour (a synestia) would mix the two bodies thoroughly and so explain their matching compositions.

perspectives.holder: Multiple-impact model
perspectives.account: The Moon was built up from a series of smaller impacts rather than one giant collision.

perspectives.holder: Immediate-satellite model (Kegerreis et al. 2022; NASA and Durham University simulations)
perspectives.account: High-resolution simulations show a giant impact can place a Moon-sized satellite directly into orbit within hours, with outer layers about 60 percent proto-Earth material, easing the isotope problem.

perspectives.holder: Timing of the Moon-forming impact
perspectives.account: NASA, from Apollo rock ages, gives roughly 60 million years after the Solar System began; hafnium-tungsten estimates span about 40 to 150 million years, and the chronometer depends on model assumptions.

records.title: Cambrian explosion
records.summary: From about 539 million years ago, almost every major animal body plan appears in the fossil record within some 20 to 30 million years, captured in rare soft-tissue fossil beds in Yunnan, North Greenland and the Canadian Rockies. Why it happened is still debated.
records.card: The Cambrian explosion is the burst of animal diversification that begins at the base of the Cambrian Period, dated by the International Commission on Stratigraphy to 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago. Over roughly 20 to 30 million years, arthropods, molluscs, brachiopods, worms and the first vertebrates appear, together with active predators, deep burrowers and complex eyes. Exceptionally preserved fossils at Chengjiang, Sirius Passet and the Burgess Shale show these early marine communities in unusual anatomical detail.
records.what:
The Cambrian explosion is the interval in which the fossil record changes from sparse, mostly soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms and simple trails to diverse animals belonging to most living phyla. The International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) places the base of the Cambrian Period, and of the Phanerozoic Eon, at 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago (Ma) on its current chart (v2026/06); the 2022 and 2023 charts gave the same age with ± 0.2 million years. Zircon dates from Namibia bracket the boundary at 538.6 to 538.8 Ma and indicate that the last Ediacaran-type fossils and the first complex Cambrian burrows are separated by less than about 410,000 years.

Trace fossils record the first stage: the number of burrow types jumps in the Fortunian Age (about 539 to 529 Ma), and in Age 2 (about 529 to 521 Ma) burrowers first mixed seafloor mud thoroughly. On the Siberian Platform, skeletal stem-group molluscs and brachiopods diversify through the Terreneuvian, while their crown groups radiate from about 522 Ma. Three Lagerstätten, deposits that preserve soft tissue, show the animals themselves. The Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, has a maximum age of 518.03 ± 0.71 Ma and records at least 16 phyla and about 196 species, vertebrates among them; UNESCO's 2012 inscription uses an older figure of 530 Ma. The Sirius Passet biota of Peary Land, North Greenland, about 519 Ma (Cambrian Stage 3), is dominated by predators and swimmers that lived in water very low in oxygen. The Burgess Shale on Fossil Ridge in Yoho National Park, British Columbia, found by Charles Walcott in 1909, is younger, about 505 Ma, and records the middle Cambrian tail of the radiation.

Specialists disagree on its tempo and causes: some see two phases separated by the Sinsk extinction around 513 Ma, others a protracted process of more than 22 million years or one of several radiations reaching back to about 571 Ma, while molecular clocks place animal origins well before the first fossils. Proposed causes, often combined, are rising oxygen, escalating predator–prey ecology and new developmental gene networks.

uncertainty.note: Start is the ICS base of the Cambrian, 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma; Zhuravlev & Wood (2018) place the onset of skeletal diversification at about 542 Ma, and Wood et al. (2019) see earlier radiations from about 571 Ma. End is the Sinsk extinction, about 513 Ma (Zhuravlev & Wood 2018); Wood et al. (2019) bound the explosion at about 520 Ma, while the Burgess Shale (about 505 Ma) and the continuation into the Ordovician radiation extend the tail later.

records.how: Sequence and mechanism as currently reconstructed: (1) By the late Ediacaran, from about 571 Ma, soft-bodied macro-organisms and simple bilaterian trails already existed on seafloors bound by microbial mats, and drill holes in the tube fossil Cloudina show predation before the Cambrian began. (2) Across the boundary at 538.8 Ma the Ediacaran biota disappears within a window of about 410,000 years and complex probing burrows such as Treptichnus pedum spread; in the Fortunian the diversity of burrow forms rises faster than at any other time. (3) In Age 2 deep burrowing and sediment mixing replace mat-bound seafloors (the agronomic revolution), pushing oxygen and food into the sediment and opening new niches. (4) Mineralised skeletons, jointed limbs, eyes and active predation spread, and food webs gain tiers; Chengjiang and Sirius Passet show predator-rich communities by about 519 to 518 Ma, some living in water with only 0.2 to 0.4 ml of oxygen per litre. (5) The Sinsk event around 513 Ma removes many stem groups, including archaeocyath reefs, while crown-group lineages continue into the Ordovician. Soft tissues survive at the Lagerstätten because animals were buried in fine, low-oxygen mud below storm wave base, at the Burgess Shale probably by underwater mudflows. Proposed drivers are rising oxygen that made energetically costly carnivory possible, escalating predator–prey and engineering feedbacks, developmental gene regulatory networks assembled tens of millions of years earlier, and pulses of redox and nutrient change; most authors combine several.
records.why_it_matters: The Cambrian explosion set out the basic anatomical designs of most animal phyla living today, including the chordate line that leads to fish and, much later, to humans; the early vertebrates of Chengjiang are among its oldest known members. It also assembled the first ecosystems that look modern: predators and prey, burrowers that mixed and ventilated the seafloor, and food webs several tiers deep, which changed how carbon and nutrients cycle through the oceans. Its starting point is the base of the Phanerozoic Eon, so the geological time scale used by every later record on this globe is anchored to it, and later crises and recoveries, from the Sinsk event to the Ordovician radiation and the end-Permian extinction, are measured against the body plans established here. The Lagerstätten matter in their own right: without the rare soft-tissue windows of Chengjiang, Sirius Passet and the Burgess Shale, the radiation would be known almost only from shells and burrows, and the long argument over whether animals arose suddenly or had hidden earlier histories would lack its central evidence. If the molecular-clock view of deep roots is correct, the event records less the birth of animals than the moment they became large, mobile, armoured and fossilisable. Today the Burgess Shale and Chengjiang are protected World Heritage properties whose fossils remain a principal test of how environment and ecology steer evolution.

perspectives.holder: Oxygenation as environmental trigger (e.g. Sperling et al. 2013; Wood et al. 2019)
perspectives.account: Rising and fluctuating ocean oxygen and nutrient supply are argued to have enabled the radiation: in modern low-oxygen zones carnivores are scarce, so oxygen thresholds may have gated predation and complex food webs, explaining the timing; Wood and colleagues tie successive radiations to dynamic redox changes.

perspectives.holder: Tolerance of low oxygen challenges a simple oxygen trigger (e.g. Hammarlund et al. 2019; Mángano & Buatois 2020)
perspectives.account: Geochemistry at Sirius Passet indicates a diverse predator community living at roughly 0.2 to 0.4 ml of oxygen per litre, and trace-fossil workers argue early animals tolerated dysoxia and may have helped raise oxygen themselves, so oxygen is seen as permissive rather than the fundamental trigger.

perspectives.holder: Ecological escalation and ecosystem engineering (e.g. Linnemann et al. 2019; Mángano & Buatois 2020; Harper et al. 2019)
perspectives.account: Predator–prey arms races and the spread of mobile burrowers drove ecological cascades: the Ediacaran-to-Cambrian faunal turnover within about 410,000 years, the replacement of mat seafloors by mixed sediment, and predator-dominated communities point to feedbacks among animals themselves as the engine of diversification.

perspectives.holder: Developmental genetics and deep roots (e.g. Erwin et al. 2011; dos Reis et al. 2015)
perspectives.account: Molecular clocks and comparative developmental data suggest animal lineages and their gene regulatory toolkits arose in the Cryogenian or Ediacaran, tens of millions of years before their first fossils; the explosion is then an ecological and preservational release of pre-existing lineages, though clock precision is too low to match dates to specific environmental events.

perspectives.holder: Tempo: one burst versus a protracted or multi-phase radiation (e.g. Zhuravlev & Wood 2018; Yang et al. 2018; Wood et al. 2019)
perspectives.account: Rather than a single short event, the radiation is described as two phases separated by the Sinsk extinction near 513 Ma, as a process lasting more than 22 million years up to Chengjiang time, or as one of several transitional radiations from the late Ediacaran into the early Palaeozoic.

records.title: Chicxulub impact and the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction
records.summary: About 66.04 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide struck the shallow sea off Yucatán, triggering the mass extinction that ended the age of the dinosaurs.
records.card: An asteroid about 10 km across hit a carbonate-rich shallow sea at what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, leaving a buried crater some 180–200 km wide. Soot, dust and sulfur thrown into the atmosphere darkened and cooled the planet, and more than 60% of species died out within a geologically brief interval. The extinction marks the boundary between the Cretaceous and the Paleogene, and between the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras.
records.what:
Roughly 66.04 million years ago an asteroid struck the southern Gulf of Mexico, at a point now on the northern coast of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Modelling of the crater's buried structure indicates it came in from the northeast at a steep angle of about 45–60 degrees. It hit a sea floor built of carbonate and sulfate rock several kilometres thick, and within minutes excavated and collapsed into a multi-ring crater roughly 180–200 km across, with a central ring of peaks formed from uplifted basement rock capped by melt rock. Seawater surged back into the crater within the hour, and a tsunami reflected from the rim reached the centre within about a day, leaving sand, gravel and charcoal from burning forests.

Ejecta spread across the whole planet. Near the crater it forms breccias tens to hundreds of metres thick; around the Gulf it includes tsunami and slump deposits; far away it is a thin clay layer rich in iridium, shocked quartz and glass spherules. Soot, rock dust and an estimated 100–500 gigatonnes of sulfur lofted into the atmosphere blocked sunlight and cooled the climate, collapsing photosynthesis on land and in the oceans. More than 60% of Cretaceous species disappeared, among them the non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, marine reptiles, ammonites and many groups of marine plankton.

Argon dating places the K–Pg boundary at about 66.043 million years ago and shows the impact and the extinction coincide within about 32,000 years; older publications give 65.0 or 65.5 million years because of earlier calibrations. Scientists agree the impact happened at the boundary; a minority still argues that the Deccan Traps eruptions in India were the main driver of the extinction, while most recent studies find the impact alone coincides with the extinction pulse.

The crater is buried beneath younger sediments. It was identified in 1991 from gravity and magnetic anomalies and oil-well cores, and was later cored through its peak ring by IODP–ICDP Expedition 364.

uncertainty.note: Impact age ±0.010–0.011 Ma is analytical (1σ); a different Fish Canyon sanidine standard age could shift 40Ar/39Ar dates by up to ~200 kyr (Schoene et al. 2021). The end bound is the upper limit of impact–extinction synchrony (within 32 kyr, Renne et al. 2013), not a measured extinction duration.

records.how: The impactor, estimated at about 10 km in diameter, struck at a steep angle (about 45–60°) from the northeast into a 3–4 km thick sequence of carbonate and sulfate-bearing sedimentary rock. The transient crater was about 100 km wide; within minutes its uplifted centre collapsed outward to form a peak ring, giving a final crater of about 180–200 km. Earthquakes far stronger than any recorded today, Gulf-wide tsunamis and slumping followed. Ejecta, some of it thrown out at several kilometres per second, rained back worldwide as spherules, shocked quartz and an iridium-rich clay; re-entering ejecta may have heated the atmosphere and ignited wildfires, as charcoal in the crater infill suggests. The vaporised target released an estimated 100–500 Gt of sulfur, which formed sunlight-absorbing aerosols, along with soot and dust. The resulting darkness and cooling suppressed photosynthesis, collapsing food chains from plankton upward; a sharp carbon-isotope excursion records the disruption of the carbon cycle, whose atmospheric part probably recovered in under about 5,000 years.
records.why_it_matters:
The Chicxulub impact closed the Mesozoic Era. By removing the non-avian dinosaurs and many marine groups, it emptied ecological roles that surviving lineages, including the mammals, filled during the Paleogene; the modern dominance of mammals, and so the eventual evolution of primates and humans, sits downstream of that turnover. Had the asteroid missed, or struck deep ocean crust rather than a sulfur- and carbonate-rich shelf, the climatic shock would likely have been very different, and the dinosaur-dominated ecosystems of the late Cretaceous might have persisted.

The event also changed science. The 1980 discovery of an iridium spike in boundary clay launched the impact hypothesis; locating the crater in 1991 turned a controversial idea into one of the best-tested causal explanations in Earth history, and showed that sudden external catastrophes, not only slow change, shape life's history. Its details mattered too: modelling suggests that a steep impact like this one releases more climate-changing gas per unit of impactor mass than a grazing or vertical strike would have. The boundary layer it laid down is the global marker geologists use to define the start of the Cenozoic.

records.title: Out of Africa dispersal of Homo sapiens
records.summary: Between roughly 70,000 and 45,000 years ago, a population of Homo sapiens left Africa and spread across Eurasia to Australia; nearly all ancestry of people living outside Africa today traces back to it.
records.card: Genomes of living people show that almost everyone outside Africa descends mainly from one population that left the continent after a bottleneck, which genetic studies date to between about 72,000 and 50,000 years ago. Its members interbred with Neanderthals about 50,500–43,500 years ago and, in the ancestry of Papuans and Aboriginal Australians, with Denisovans. Earlier exits, such as the one recorded at Misliya Cave in Israel, left little trace, and the route and the date of arrival in Australia are still argued.
records.what:
Out of Africa refers to the dispersal of Homo sapiens from Africa into Eurasia and on to Sahul, the Pleistocene landmass joining Australia and New Guinea. Genomes of present-day people show that nearly all ancestry outside Africa traces to one founding population that left the continent and passed through a population bottleneck. Malaspinas and colleagues (2016) dated that bottleneck to about 72,000 years ago (95% interval 60,000–104,000) and the split of the ancestors of Aboriginal Australians and Papuans from Eurasians to about 58,000 years ago (51,000–72,000), assuming a mutation rate of 1.25 × 10⁻⁸ per site per generation and 29-year generations; other genetic studies reviewed by López and colleagues (2015) give 60,000–50,000 years. A firm minimum comes from Neanderthal DNA: most of it in non-Africans entered during one extended period of interbreeding about 50,500–43,500 years ago, so the founding population had left Africa by then and was still largely a single group.

It was not the first exit. A maxilla from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel, is dated to 177,000–194,000 years ago; Homo sapiens remains from Skhul and Qafzeh in the same region to roughly 90,000–120,000 years ago; and a partial skull from Apidima Cave in southern Greece to more than 210,000 years ago, an identification and date that other researchers dispute. Genetic results imply that such early groups were not the main ancestors of living non-Africans, although some models allow them a small share.

Scholars still disagree on the route, the number of waves and the date people reached Australia. Genetic studies have been read as favouring either a southern crossing of the Bab el-Mandeb strait into Arabia or a northern exit through Egypt and Sinai, and a date of about 65,000 years for first occupation at Madjedbebe in northern Australia conflicts with arguments for arrival nearer 50,000 years ago. By about 45,000 years ago, descendants of the dispersal were living from central Europe to western Siberia, and Sahul had been settled.

uncertainty.note: Start: genetic estimates for the founding bottleneck and exit range from ~72 ka (95% CI 60–104 ka; Malaspinas et al. 2016) to 60–50 ka (studies reviewed by López et al. 2015; 50–55 ka preferred by O'Connell et al. 2018); all depend on assumed mutation rates and generation times. End: by ~45 ka H. sapiens of this lineage were at Ust'-Ishim (46,880–43,210 cal BP) and Ranis (43,400–46,580 cal BP), and Sahul was settled by 47.5–55 ka. Earlier dispersals (Apidima >210 ka, Misliya 177–194 ka, Skhul/Qafzeh ~90–120 ka) are outside this span by design. Years are counted back from the present; the 1950 vs 2026 reference difference is negligible at this precision.

records.how: The dispersal was a slow spread of small foraging groups over thousands of years, not a planned migration. (1) Climate opened and closed corridors: Groucutt and colleagues link expansions to humid phases, in Marine Isotope Stage 5 (~125–75 ka) and again in Stage 3 (~55–45 ka), when parts of Arabia turned to grassland and savanna. (2) Lower sea levels, about 100 m below today at the deepest Late Pleistocene regression, narrowed water gaps and exposed the Sunda and Sahul shelves, but Wallacea was never joined to either, so reaching Sahul needed open-sea voyages along island routes of 1,000–1,500 km, with at least one crossing longer than 70 km. (3) The founding groups were small: genomes from Ranis and Zlatý kůň imply an effective population of about 300 around 45,000 years ago. (4) As they spread, they met and interbred with archaic humans: one extended period of Neanderthal gene flow, about 50,500–43,500 years ago, shared by all non-Africans, after which harmful Neanderthal variants were quickly lost; and later Denisovan admixture, about 44,000 years ago, in the ancestors of Papuans and Aboriginal Australians. (5) Populations then diverged regionally: European and East Asian ancestors split about 42,000 years ago (29,000–55,000) in the Malaspinas model, and Papuan and Aboriginal Australian ancestors about 37,000 years ago. Absolute genetic dates rest on assumed mutation rates; pedigree-based rates roughly double divergence dates compared with older phylogenetic rates.
records.why_it_matters: This dispersal produced the ancestors of nearly every person whose family history lies outside Africa, so the population history of Asia, Australia, the Pacific, Europe and the Americas begins with it. It also explains part of the shape of human genetic variation: people outside Africa carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA from one shared period of interbreeding, with variants that still affect immune function, skin pigmentation and metabolism, and Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry about 4% Denisovan ancestry. The settlement of Sahul by about 50,000 years ago, and possibly earlier, required repeated open-sea crossings of Wallacea, evidence that seafaring was within the reach of Pleistocene foragers. The event matters too as a test case for how science dates the deep past, because genetic clocks, radiocarbon, luminescence and fossils must all be reconciled, and the Madjedbebe debate shows how much the answer depends on the method. The counterfactual is visible in the record itself: earlier groups of Homo sapiens reached the Levant and possibly Greece more than 100,000 years before, but they did not become the main ancestors of living people. Had the later dispersal faded out as the earlier ones did, Eurasia would have remained, for longer at least, the domain of Neanderthals, Denisovans and other archaic humans, and the ancestry of most living people would be very different.

related.because: The dispersing population descended from Homo sapiens that had evolved in Africa, and its members carried the African ancestry that all non-Africans share.

perspectives.holder: Southern-route models: many mtDNA studies and coastal 'beachcomber' serial-bottleneck models, as reviewed by López et al. (2015)
perspectives.account: The main dispersal left the Horn of Africa across the Bab el-Mandeb into southern Arabia and moved along the coasts toward South Asia; Groucutt and others reply that mtDNA lineage geography alone cannot settle the route.

perspectives.holder: Pagani et al. (2015), from 225 Egyptian and Ethiopian genomes
perspectives.account: Non-African haplotypes are closer to Egyptian than to Ethiopian ones, and Egyptians split from non-Africans later (~55 kya) than Ethiopians (~65 kya), favouring a predominantly northern exit through Egypt and Sinai.

perspectives.holder: Early-and-multiple dispersal models: Groucutt et al. (2015); Hershkovitz et al. (2018) for Misliya; Harvati et al. (2019) for Apidima
perspectives.account: Homo sapiens left Africa repeatedly from at least 177,000–194,000 years ago, during humid windows, and the later successful expansion largely swamped earlier ones; Apidima 1 (>210 ka) is offered as evidence of multiple dispersals.

perspectives.holder: Critics of the Apidima 1 date and attribution, reported in 2019 coverage
perspectives.account: Raw U-series results spread over a wide range and the fragment may be considerably younger than 210,000 years; co-author Rainer Grün replied that the younger samples differ chemically from the skull.

perspectives.holder: Late single-dispersal view: O'Connell et al. (2018); supported for population structure by Sümer et al. (2024) and Malaspinas et al. (2016)
perspectives.account: The successful dispersal was a single movement about 50,000–55,000 years ago; Homo sapiens remains older than about 50,000 years outside Africa belong to other populations, and Malaspinas found a single exit supported once archaic admixture is modelled, though modern genomes alone also fit two waves.

perspectives.holder: Clarkson et al. (2017), Madjedbebe excavators
perspectives.account: Artefacts in primary context, with refits and optical dates, show people at Madjedbebe from around 65,000 years ago, setting a new minimum age for the dispersal out of Africa.

perspectives.holder: O'Connell et al. (2018)
perspectives.account: Artefacts likely moved down through the sand sheet by termites, rain-splash and creep, so the optical dates overstate their age; Sahul was first colonised around 48,000–50,000 years ago.

perspectives.holder: Westaway et al. (2017) versus O'Connell et al. (2018) on Lida Ajer
perspectives.account: Westaway's team dates modern human teeth in Sumatra to 73,000–63,000 years ago; O'Connell's team accepts this as the strongest pre-50 ka case but questions where the teeth originally lay in the deposit.

records.title: Classic Maya period
records.summary: From about 250 to 900 CE, rival dynasties of divine lords ruled dozens of Maya city-states in the tropical lowlands of Mesoamerica, raising stone stelae dated in the Long Count, before most southern cities were abandoned.
records.card: The Classic period is the era of dated royal monuments in the Maya lowlands of today's Guatemala, Mexico, Belize and Honduras, conventionally c. 250–900 CE. Kingdoms such as Tikal, Calakmul's Kaan dynasty, Copán, Palenque and Caracol fought, allied and recorded their histories in hieroglyphic texts. Lidar suggests millions of people lived there in the eighth century; by around 1000 CE the southern cities stood largely empty, after drought, war and economic change.
records.what:
The Classic period is the span in which lowland Maya kings recorded their reigns on carved stone monuments dated with the Long Count calendar. A chronology following Coe (1987) places it from about 250 to 900 CE, with a Late Classic peak from about 600 to 800; other scholars write 300–900 or 300–1000 CE, so both boundaries are conventions rather than events. Tikal's earliest dated sculpture, Stela 29, carries a date in 292 CE and its last, Stela 11, one in 869; the latest Long Count date on any monument, at Toniná in Mexico, falls in 909.

Political life centred on kingdoms ruled by divine lords. Tikal (Mutal) in Guatemala's Petén records 33 rulers. In 378 CE a figure named Sihyaj K'ahk', linked to the central Mexican metropolis of Teotihuacan, arrived at Tikal on the day its king died, and a new line took the throne; whether this was a conquest is still argued. A lord from the Tikal region founded Copán's 16-ruler dynasty in 427. From the sixth century the Kaan (snake) dynasty, later seated at Calakmul, built a rival network: Tikal was defeated in 562 and fell silent for some 130 years, Palenque was attacked in 599 and 611, and Tikal answered by defeating Calakmul in 695. Women sometimes held power: Lady Yohl Ik'nal ruled Palenque for 21 years before the long reign of K'inich Janaab Pakal (615–683).

The 2016 lidar survey of northern Guatemala mapped 61,480 structures and implies 7–11 million people across the central lowlands in 650–800 CE, with causeways, wetland field systems, upland terraces and defensive earthworks. During the Terminal Classic, about 800–1000 CE, the southern cities lost their kings and most of their people. Scholars disagree on why: some give drought the leading role, others stress warfare, land degradation and a shift of trade to coastal sea routes. Dates here use the Goodman–Martínez–Thompson correlation; its variants (584283, 584285, 584286) differ by a few days.

uncertainty.note: Period boundaries are scholarly conventions: 250–900 CE (Coe 1987 chronology), 300–900 CE (Kennett et al. 2013; UNESCO Copán listing), 300–1000 CE (Kennett et al. 2012), Classic 300–800 plus Terminal Classic 800–1000 CE (Turner & Sabloff 2012). All Long Count conversions depend on the GMT correlation; the 584283 and 584285 constants differ by two days, so a date such as 8.17.1.4.12 is 14 January 378 (584283) or 16 January 378 (584285) in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (13 or 15 January Julian). Skidmore (2010) gives Palenque dates in the Julian calendar under 584285; Kennett et al. (2013) give 6 August 695, which is Gregorian under 584283.

records.how: The Classic order rested on three foundations. First, a farming landscape engineered at scale: lidar shows about 362 km² of deliberately modified farmland in the surveyed area, wetland field systems that imply central planning, upland terraces managed by households, and some 106 km of causeways linking settlements. Second, divine kingship expressed in writing and calendars: rulers commissioned stelae, lintels and stairways whose texts used the Long Count, a day count from a base date of 13.0.0.0.0 4 Ajaw 8 Kumk'u, and by 600–900 CE this practice had spread to more than 40 lowland centres. Third, a competitive political system in which dynasties made patron–client alliances and fought: the Kaan kingdom built a network of allies against Tikal, Caracol's K'an II fought Naranjo as its ally, and defensive earthworks spread across the landscape. Climate set the stage. A stalagmite record from Yok Balum Cave in southern Belize shows unusually wet conditions from 440 to 660 CE, matched by population growth and more political centres, then a long drying trend from 660 to 1000 CE marked by fragmentation and more warfare. Gypsum from Lake Chichancanab implies that annual rainfall fell by 41–54% during the Terminal Classic droughts. Heavy forest clearance, soil erosion and scarce fuel and timber added stress, while long-distance trade shifted to sea routes around the Yucatán Peninsula, draining wealth from the inland kingdoms. As kings failed to deliver, people left the southern cities over the ninth and tenth centuries.
records.why_it_matters: The Classic Maya kept a written, dated political history. Because their monuments carry Long Count dates, and radiocarbon dating of a Tikal lintel has confirmed the standard correlation with the European calendar, events at Tikal, Palenque or Copán can be placed on a single day. The texts give names and deeds to individual kings and queens, including women such as Lady Yohl Ik'nal who ruled in their own right, and the 1952 discovery of Pakal's tomb at Palenque counts among the greatest finds of Mexican archaeology. The lidar results changed the picture of tropical civilisation: a forest long assumed to support only scattered farming held an estimated 7–11 million people, linked by causeways and fed by engineered fields. The period's end is just as consequential. Population in the central lowlands fell by close to 90%, and the region stayed largely empty for more than a thousand years; old-growth forest returned within a few centuries, and Tikal and Calakmul now lie in the Maya Forest, the second-largest expanse of tropical forest in the Americas. Turner and Sabloff find that the interior was never reoccupied, even after forests and soils recovered, because once trade had turned to the coasts it offered no commercial advantage; had trade stayed inland, the Petén might well have filled again. The collapse is now studied as a case of how drought, land use and economic change interact, a lesson those authors explicitly draw for present-day sustainability.

perspectives.holder: Kennett et al. (2012), Science; Evans et al. (2018), Science
perspectives.account: Climate was a major driver: a wet interval (440–660 CE) favoured growth and political expansion, a drying trend from 660 CE accompanied fragmentation and warfare, and Terminal Classic droughts cut annual rainfall by about 41–54% (up to 70% at peak), stressing maize farming.

perspectives.holder: Turner and Sabloff (2012), PNAS
perspectives.account: The collapse was a coupled human–environment process: deforestation, erosion and fuel scarcity, amplified by aridity, interacted with intercity conflict and, most importantly in their view, a shift of trade to sea routes around the peninsula; people moved away for better opportunities, and there is little evidence of mass famine.

perspectives.holder: Canuto et al. (2018), Science (PACUNAM Lidar Initiative)
perspectives.account: Widespread, sizeable defensive features in the lidar data point to societal disconnection and large-scale conflict, giving warfare a larger structural role in the Late Classic landscape than earlier site-based surveys showed.

perspectives.holder: David Stuart (1998 extract; UT Austin 2020); many archaeologists per UT Austin
perspectives.account: Sihyaj K'ahk' came from or on behalf of Teotihuacan, possibly with an army, and his arrival in 378 coincided with the death of Tikal's king and the installation of a new dynasty; Stuart proposes that Spearthrower Owl was Teotihuacan's ruler. The conquest reading remains debated, and Stuart himself flagged parts of it as speculative.

perspectives.holder: Martin and Skidmore (2012); Kennett et al. (2013)
perspectives.account: The Goodman–Martínez–Thompson family of correlations is accepted; 584283 and 584285 are the most widely used constants, Martin and Skidmore argue for 584286, and radiocarbon dating of Tikal Temple I Lintel 3 strongly supports the GMT family while ruling out constants centuries away.

records.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
records.summary: Between the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376 and the deposition of the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna in 476, the western half of the Roman Empire lost its provinces, its capital city's security and finally its emperors, while the eastern half survived.
records.card: A century of crises broke Roman rule in the West: Goths fleeing the Huns destroyed an imperial army at Adrianople in 378, Rome itself was sacked in 410 and 455, and the Vandals took the rich African provinces. In 476 the officer Odoacer killed the general Orestes, deposed his young son Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy as a king. Historians still argue whether this was a catastrophic collapse or a slower transformation, and whether 476 is the right end date at all.
records.what:
The fall of the Western Roman Empire is the name given to the loss of imperial government in the Latin-speaking western provinces during the late fourth and fifth centuries CE. In 376, Gothic Tervingi under Fritigern and Alavivus, displaced by the Huns, asked the eastern emperor Valens for admission and were ferried across the lower Danube. Starved and exploited by the Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus, they revolted near Marcianopolis, and on 9 August 378 (Julian) they destroyed Valens' army near Adrianople; the emperor was killed and, by Ammianus Marcellinus' account, barely a third of his force escaped.

After Theodosius I died in 395 the empire was governed as eastern and western halves. The western court withdrew from Milan to Ravenna in 402; Vandals, Alans, Suevi and Burgundians crossed the Rhine at the end of 406; Britain slipped out of imperial control; and in 410 Alaric's Goths entered Rome through the Salarian Gate and plundered it. By 439 the Vandals held Carthage and nearly all of Roman North Africa. In 455, after the murders of Valentinian III and Petronius Maximus, the Vandal king Gaiseric sacked Rome for about two weeks and carried the empress Eudoxia and her daughters to Carthage.

In 475 the general Orestes drove the emperor Julius Nepos to Dalmatia and raised his own son Romulus, nicknamed Augustulus. In August 476 troops in Italy proclaimed Odoacer king; he killed Orestes near Placentia, killed Orestes' brother Paulus at Ravenna, and on or soon after 4 September deposed Romulus, sparing him with a pension and sending him to Campania. The imperial regalia went to Zeno in Constantinople, and the eastern empire continued. Writers of the sixth century such as Marcellinus Comes and Jordanes treated 476 as the end of the western empire. Modern historians disagree about whether the process was a violent collapse or a gradual transformation, and some argue that Nepos, who lived until 480, was the last legitimate western emperor.

uncertainty.note: Start = the Gothic crossing of the Danube (376). End = the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, dated by Mathisen to on or soon after 4 September 476 (Julian), i.e. 5 September 476 proleptic Gregorian; Paulus was killed on 31 August or 4 September, so the exact day is not fixed. Mathisen argues the western line properly ends with the death of Julius Nepos in 480, hence end_plus_years 4. The choice of start date is a convention: Heather dates the final collapse of imperial structures to 468–476.

records.how: Causes and sequence. (1) External pressure: the Huns' arrival north of the Black Sea in 375 drove Gothic groups to seek refuge in Roman territory, and in 376 Valens allowed the Tervingi across the Danube. Supply failure and the greed of the commanders Lupicinus and Maximus turned refugees into rebels by 377. (2) Military shock: at Adrianople on 9 August 378 Valens attacked before his nephew Gratian's western army arrived; Gothic cavalry routed the Roman horse, the crowded infantry broke in the afternoon heat, and Valens died. A modern estimate cited by Lenski puts Roman dead near 26,000 of about 40,000. (3) Political division and weak centre: after 395 the halves were ruled separately; the western court sat at Ravenna from 402, generals such as Stilicho and Aetius dominated emperors, and both were murdered (408 and 454). (4) Loss of territory and taxes: the Rhine crossing of 406, the loss of Britain, the sack of Rome in 410 and the Vandal conquest of North Africa by 439 removed provinces whose agricultural taxes paid the army; Heather describes a downward spiral in which lost land meant lost revenue and fewer troops. (5) Endgame: after 455 western emperors were made and unmade by army commanders. Orestes raised his son in 475; on 23 August 476 the troops in Italy proclaimed Odoacer, an officer of Scirian and Hunnic background by one account, as their king. Odoacer killed Orestes and Paulus, deposed Romulus, sent the regalia east and governed Italy as a king while the eastern emperor remained the nominal sovereign. Explanations differ: Gibbon stressed internal decay, Heather external pressure, Ward-Perkins violent invasion and chance, and the 'transformation' school continuity.
records.why_it_matters: The deposition of 476 ended the line of emperors resident in the western Mediterranean, and Jordanes, writing in 551, already treated it as the moment from which Gothic kings held Rome and Italy. Odoacer ruled Italy as a king for about thirteen years until Theodoric's Ostrogoths replaced him in 493, and across the former western provinces landowners had to adapt to local Germanic kings backed by armed followings, the political frame of early medieval western Europe. The consequences went beyond politics. Heather argues that when the imperial bureaucracy disappeared, so did the careers that had sustained elite literacy, and that without powerful western emperors the later papacy as a monarchy is hard to imagine. Ward-Perkins points to a sharp fall in material comfort and in everyday reading and writing across the West. Meanwhile the eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, survived, so Roman imperial government carried on in the eastern Mediterranean under Zeno and his successors. The fall also shaped how later centuries thought about empires: Gibbon read it as a lesson in the decay that follows overextension, and modern historians remain split between those who stress collapse and those who stress transformation. Counterfactuals are built into that debate: Heather and Ward-Perkins both stress chance events such as the arrival of the Huns, so had the Huns not pushed the Goths across the Danube in 376 the western empire might have lasted far longer, and Ward-Perkins argues that the East survived largely because a strait of sea shielded its richest provinces, something the West did not have.

perspectives.holder: Edward Gibbon, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 38 ('General Observations')
perspectives.account: The fall was the natural result of overextension: prosperity bred decay, the division of the empire weakened the West, reliance on barbarian troops corrupted discipline, and Christianity drew energy and wealth away from civic and military life.

perspectives.holder: The 'transformation' school associated with Peter Brown (the 'Reformers' in O'Donnell's terms)
perspectives.account: Late antiquity should be read as a long transformation rather than an end, with weight on continuity, the surviving East, and religious and cultural change; O'Donnell counts himself among this group.

perspectives.holder: Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire: A New History (2005)
perspectives.account: Internal decline does not explain the fifth-century collapse; Hunnic pressure pushed larger, more unified Germanic groups into the empire, and lost territory meant lost taxes and armies in a spiral that ended imperial structures in the West between 468 and 476.

perspectives.holder: Bryan Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
perspectives.account: The end of Roman rule was violent and painful, and archaeology shows a steep fall in material comfort and literacy; 476 itself matters little because the last western emperors had already lost real power, and the East survived mainly through the shelter of its geography.

perspectives.holder: Ralph W. Mathisen (De Imperatoribus Romanis) versus Geoffrey S. Nathan and most scholars
perspectives.account: Mathisen argues that Julius Nepos, recognised in the East and still minting coins in Odoacer's Italy, was the last legitimate western emperor until his death in 480; Nathan notes that most scholars take Romulus' deposition in 476 as the end of the western empire as a political entity.

records.title: Ming Great Wall
records.summary: Between 1368 and 1644 the Ming dynasty built an 8,852 km frontier line of walls, trenches, towers and passes from Liaoning to Gansu, mostly in surges driven by Mongol raids; its brick-faced eastern sections are the Great Wall most people picture.
records.card: The Ming at first held the northern frontier with forts and passes, and only from 1437 joined them with continuous wall. Building peaked between 1465 and 1566 as Mongol raids grew, and after Altan Khan broke through near Gubeikou in 1550, Qi Jiguang lined the wall near Beijing with about 1,200 hollow brick towers. China's 2012 survey measures the Ming line at 8,851.8 km, including trenches and natural barriers.
records.what:
The Ming Great Wall is the frontier line built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) across northern China, and the wall most visitors picture. China's 2012 survey measured it at 8,851.8 km: 6,259.6 km of built wall, 359.7 km of trench and 2,232.5 km of ridges, rivers and other natural barriers worked into the line, with 17,449 towers and other single structures and 1,272 passes and forts. The main line runs from Hushan in eastern Liaoning to Jiayuguan in Gansu.

It was never one project. A 2024 study combining Ming records, field survey and GIS divides it into five phases. Under the first emperors (1368–1435) the frontier was held by 453 forts and passes, among them Jiayuguan (1372) and Shanhaiguan (1381), and no continuous wall. The first continuous wall rose in Liaodong between 1437 and 1442. After the Ming army's defeat by the Mongols at Tumu in 1449 the court moved from attack to defence, and between 1465 and 1521 the frontier districts built about 5,400 km of wall; Badaling's fort dates from 1505. A second surge came under the Jiajing emperor (1522–1566), when Mongol raids were heaviest: about 1,340 km of new wall and 3,780 km of rebuilding, including the whole Jizhou line near Beijing in 1551. In 1550 Altan Khan's cavalry broke through near Gubeikou and plundered the countryside around Beijing for three days. From 1568 Qi Jiguang rebuilt the Jizhou wall with hollow brick towers, about 1,200 of them, finished in 1571. After a peace with Altan Khan in the Longqing reign, building slowed; the last new walls went up in the north-west, and Liaodong repaired 1,050 km of wall in 1608 against the rising Jurchens. In 1644 the Qing army entered through Shanhaiguan and the Ming fell.

Figures differ by method. ICOMOS in 1987 gave 5,650 km of crenellated wall with 25,000 towers; the survey's larger total counts trenches, branch lines and natural barriers.

uncertainty.note: Bounded by the dynasty. Continuous wall-building began in 1437; Yang et al. (2024) find no large-scale construction after 1620, hence the end_minus range.

records.how: The Ming built forts, passes and beacon piers first and only later joined them with wall. In the east the wall is a core of rubble and loess faced with brick and dressed stone, or built entirely of stone, with a walkway and crenellations; in the west it is mostly rammed earth. The line belonged to a layered system: nine, later eleven, frontier military districts (Zhenbao and Chang were added to protect the capital and the imperial tombs), about 1,100 garrisons ranked in five levels (zhen, lu, wei, suo, bao), and thousands of posts, beacon towers and relay stations. Construction was organised by district and assigned to garrison troops section by section. When Qi Jiguang took over Jizhou in 1568 he argued that walls repaired every year simply fell down again, and proposed towers straddling the wall, 5 zhang tall, hollow, in three storeys, each holding 100 men with armour, weapons and grain; he asked for 1,200 to be built first and, finding the frontier troops undisciplined, brought in soldiers from Zhejiang. The towers were finished in the autumn of 1571. At Zhuizi Mountain on the Liaoning–Hebei border, a section first built in 1381, the surviving wall is 1.5–4.3 m wide and up to 9.8 m high.
records.why_it_matters: The Ming wall is the Great Wall of popular imagination: its brick towers on the ridges north of Beijing, at Badaling, Mutianyu and Jinshanling, shape how the world pictures China's past, and Badaling alone drew more than 76.5 million visitors between 2005 and 2015. Historically it records two centuries of conflict with the Mongols. Its building surges track the raids, and it did not always hold: in 1550 Altan Khan's riders broke through near Gubeikou and plundered the capital region for three days, and in 1567 his forces killed tens of thousands of people in Shanxi. Peace came by negotiation rather than masonry, when the Longqing court enfeoffed Altan Khan and opened border markets. In 1644 Shanhaiguan, which earlier Later Jin incursions had bypassed, was opened to the Qing army, and the Ming fell. Without the Jiajing-era surge and Qi Jiguang's towers there would be no brick-towered wall around Beijing; Ming defence would have rested on the scattered forts of the early dynasty. Today the Ming wall is also a conservation problem: only about 5.8% of its length is well preserved, and over half has vanished or decayed badly.

records.title: Gutenberg's movable-type printing press at Mainz
records.summary: In the 1450s Johannes Gutenberg and his partners in Mainz turned out printed books from cast metal type in quantity, culminating in the 42-line Latin Bible of about 1454–1455; within fifty years presses operated in some 205 European cities.
records.card: Gutenberg's Mainz workshop was making schoolbooks and indulgence forms in cast type by 1454, and a 643-leaf Latin Bible in two columns of 42 lines followed by 1455, in an edition of roughly 150 copies. A lawsuit by his financier Johann Fust in November 1455 ended their partnership, and Fust and Peter Schoeffer then ran their own press. The craft left Mainz with journeymen, and by 1500 books were being printed in about 205 European cities for a fraction of their former price.
records.what:
Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1400–1468) developed in Mainz, on the Rhine, a way of printing whole books from individually cast metal letters set into pages and inked and pressed onto paper or vellum. A fifteenth-century recollection by the Cologne printer Ulrich Zel put the start in 1450, and economic historians date the first press to between 1448 and 1450. Nobody knows when Gutenberg's first usable type, a large square Gothic face known from its schoolbook and calendar fragments as the DK type, was ready. Princeton University Library's curators think Donatus grammars set in it, and a German prophetic text, were probably on sale by 1453.

The earliest firm date for European printing is 22 October 1454, on a fragment of a 31-line indulgence form issued at Erfurt. Gutenberg had contracted to print such forms in the late summer of 1454 for the Cyprus indulgence campaign, which was raising money against the Ottoman advance. In the same years his shop set the 42-line Bible: 643 large folio leaves intended to bind in two volumes, begun in 40-line columns and then changed to 42, with four compositors working on four sections at once. After eleven quires the print run was raised, and at least 120 paper and perhaps 40 vellum copies were produced, a figure that fits contemporary reports of 158 or 180 copies in 1455. Initials and headings were added by hand in colour.

Gutenberg's financier Johann Fust sued him in late 1455 over the costs of the joint 'work of the books'; the notarial record of that dispute is dated 6 November 1455. Fust then partnered with the scribe Peter Schoeffer, and their Psalter of 14 August 1457 was the first printed book to name its makers and give the date. After Mainz was captured in October 1462, workers dispersed. From 1470 to 1500 printing reached some 240 further towns, and it was the printing of books in cast type, not its first invention anywhere, that this record covers: movable type had been used earlier in Korea and China.

uncertainty.note: Start: Dittmar (2009) dates the first press to 1448–1450 and Ulrich Zel's recollection in the 1499 Cologne Chronicle says 1450; Princeton's curators think the first schoolbooks in the DK type may date to 1453 or a little earlier but call this probable, not provable. The earliest firm date is 22 October 1454 (Erfurt indulgence). End: the 42-line Bible is dated about 1454–1455 and 'probably completed late in 1455' (Library of Congress); the Harry Ransom Center gives 1454–1456.

records.how: Gutenberg's workshop made the first usable European printing type in the early 1450s, the large square Gothic DK type, and improved it into a finer text face. Type was cast in metal, set letter by letter into lines, locked into pages and printed on a press, so a page could be re-used or distributed in standing type for months. The Bible shop printed schoolbooks on vellum first, then the Cyprus indulgence forms in autumn 1454, and set the Bible by four compositors working on four sections at once. After eleven quires the edition size was raised and those quires reprinted. Fust provided loans for paper, vellum, ink and an apparatus; the dispute over those sums reached court in 1455. Printed sheets were sold across long distances, and Mainz workers later taught others, especially after the city's capture in 1462.
records.why_it_matters: A scribe, one early printer boasted, could produce in a year what a press produced in a day, and the cost fell accordingly: Dittmar finds that book prices fell by at least 65 percent between 1450 and 1500. Printing was in 205 cities by 1500. Its first economic effect is measurable: cities that gained a press in the 1400s grew about 60 percent faster in the following century than comparable cities without one. Its religious effect is also measurable: in the Holy Roman Empire, cities near a press by 1500 were far more likely to be Protestant by 1600 (Rubin). The press also changed what survived: Princeton's curators note that texts which did not reach print tended to fall rapidly out of use, while almost all school and university texts were printed. Historians disagree about how far printing itself, rather than social and political forces, drove these changes: Eisenstein stressed standardisation, while Johns showed early printed books were often unreliable and pirated. Had Gutenberg's shop failed, movable type would probably still have spread, since concurrent attempts are reported at Avignon and Haarlem and the Chinese and Korean traditions already existed; but the Mainz-centred pattern of diffusion, with journeymen leaving the Rhine for Rome, Cologne, Venice and Paris, would not have been the same.

related.title: Protestant Reformation
related.because: Rubin's analysis finds that cities with a press by 1500 were far more likely to turn Protestant by 1600, consistent with cheap print carrying reform ideas to many readers, though how far print drove the Reformation remains debated.

records.title: First voyage of Christopher Columbus
records.summary: On 12 October 1492, Christopher Columbus's expedition made landfall on the Lucayan Taíno island of Guanahaní after sailing from Palos, Spain. The transatlantic voyage initiated sustained European contact with the Americas, leading to rapid colonisation, enslavement, and devastating Indigenous demographic collapse.
records.card: Financed by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Castile and Aragon, Christopher Columbus led three ships across the Atlantic Ocean, departing Palos in August 1492 and sighting the Bahamian island of Guanahaní in October. The voyagers met Lucayan Taíno islanders, abducted several captives to serve as interpreters, and explored northern Cuba and Hispaniola before the flagship Santa María wrecked on Christmas Day. Leaving thirty-nine crewmen at the makeshift outpost of La Navidad, Columbus returned to Europe in March 1493, unleashing centuries of Spanish imperial conquest, forced labor regimes, and devastating epidemic mortality across the Caribbean.
records.what:
On 3 August 1492, Genoese mariner Christopher Columbus departed Palos de la Frontera, Andalusia, commanding three vessels—the flagship nao Santa María and caravels Pinta and Niña—chartered under the authority of the Catholic Monarchs of Castile and Aragon. The expedition paused in the Canary Islands for provisioning and repairs, setting out westward from San Sebastián de La Gomera on 6 September into the open ocean. Following thirty-three days of westward navigation, lookouts aboard the Pinta sighted land at 2:00 a.m. on 12 October 1492 (Julian calendar; 21 October proleptic Gregorian). Columbus landed later that morning on an island in the Lucayan archipelago called Guanahaní by its inhabitants, claiming it for the Crown of Castile and naming it San Salvador.

On the beach, the Spaniards encountered Lucayan people, northern relatives of the Greater Antillean Taíno. Columbus recorded their generosity, physical beauty, body paint, and lack of iron weaponry, while noting their potential as servants and converts; he detained six Indigenous islanders to carry back to Spain as interpreters. Over the following eleven weeks, guided by kidnapped captives, Columbus navigated south and west through the Bahamas, landing on northeastern Cuba on 28 October and northern Hispaniola on 6 December.

Disaster struck on the night of 24–25 December 1492 when the Santa María ran aground on a coral reef off northern Hispaniola. Aided by the Taíno cacique Guacanagaríx, the crew salvaged its timbers to build a fortified garrison named La Navidad. Columbus left thirty-nine men to garrison the fort and gather gold, departing aboard the Niña on 4 January 1493. After surviving severe winter storms that forced temporary stops in the Azores and Lisbon, Columbus anchored at Palos on 15 March 1493.

The geographical identity of Guanahaní remains debated among scholars, with San Salvador (formerly Watling Island) remaining the leading candidate alongside Samana Cay and the Plana Cays.

uncertainty.note: Exact calendar dates recorded in the ship log: departure from Palos on 3 August 1492 and return on 15 March 1493 in the Julian calendar (12 August 1492 and 24 March 1493 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar). Landfall at Guanahaní took place on 12 October 1492 Julian (21 October 1492 Gregorian).
