records.title: Troy (Hisarlık)
records.summary: A mound at Hisarlık near the Dardanelles holding superimposed settlements from about 3000 BCE to Byzantine times; its Late Bronze Age citadel is most probably the Hittites' Wilusa and the city of Homer's Iliad.
records.card: Troy is a layered settlement mound in northwest Türkiye whose levels, numbered Troy I to IX, span the Bronze Age and the Greek and Roman city of Ilion. In the Late Bronze Age a walled citadel of 2–3 ha stood here, and its excavators argue for a lower city of 25–35 ha around it, a claim critics have fiercely contested. Heinrich Schliemann's digs from 1870 made the site famous, damaged it badly, and produced the gold hoard now split between Berlin and Moscow.
records.what:
Troy is the archaeological site on the mound of Hisarlık in Çanakkale Province, northwestern Türkiye, about 4.8 km from the southern entrance to the Dardanelles. Its superimposed settlements, conventionally numbered Troy I to IX, begin about 3000 BCE and continue through the Bronze Age and the Greek and Roman city of Ilion into the late Byzantine period, giving archaeologists a reference sequence for the Aegean and Anatolia. Troy II, around 2500 BCE, had a fortified citadel with a paved ramp; the hoard Heinrich Schliemann named after King Priam came from this level, more than a thousand years before any possible Trojan War.

Troy VI, from about 1700 BCE, built a citadel of 2–3 ha inside walls of fitted limestone blocks more than 4 m thick, topped with mudbrick. Excavations led from 1988 by Manfred Korfmann found rock-cut ditches and a palisade about 400 m south of the citadel, which the excavators read as the defences of a lower city of 25–35 ha in Troy VI and VIIa. The end of Troy VIh is usually blamed on an earthquake; Troy VIIa, about 1250–1175 BCE, ended in fire.

Hittite texts name a western Anatolian kingdom, Wilusa, whose king Alaksandu concluded a treaty with Muwatalli II around 1280 BCE. Most specialists equate Wilusa with Greek Ilios and place it here, but the case rests on geography and names, since no archive has been found at the site. Greek Ilion grew on the ruins: Xerxes sacrificed to its Athena in 480 BCE, Alexander came in 334 BCE, and the terrace of a Hellenistic temple of Athena levelled the centre of the Bronze Age citadel.

Schliemann's campaigns of 1870–1890, begun on the advice of Frank Calvert, cut a trench about 14 m (45 ft) deep through the mound with little recording, destroying parts of the later levels in its path. Scholars disagree sharply about Late Bronze Age Troy: Frank Kolb and Dieter Hertel judged the lower city sparse and its reconstructions fiction, while the excavators and Easton, Hawkins and the Sherratts defended a regional capital. Whether the Iliad preserves a real war remains open.

uncertainty.note: Start is the conventional 'ca. 3000 BC' beginning of the Bronze Age sequence (Easton et al. 2002); UNESCO speaks of 4,000 years of history. Settlement continued into the late Byzantine period (Rose 2011; Jablonka & Rose 2004) and UNESCO notes Ottoman-period remains; no opened source gives a precise date for the end of habitation, so the end is set to the present, when the mound survives as a protected archaeological site (first excavated 1870; National Historical Park 1996; World Heritage 1998). Internal phase dates (Troy II c. 2500 BCE; Troy VI Late c. 1300–1250 BCE; VIIa c. 1250–1175 BCE) are pottery- and radiocarbon-based approximations.

records.how: Troy is a tell: each settlement was built on the levelled debris of the one before, on a limestone ridge rising from the alluvial plain near the mouth of the Dardanelles. The early citadels (Troy I–II) were walled and gated; after a cultural break, Troy VI introduced new architecture, grey wheelmade pottery and the first horses at the site. Its Late Bronze Age circuit wall was rebuilt section by section over generations in fitted limestone with a battered outer face, offsets and towers, on foundations deliberately left off bedrock, and fell at the end of VIh in what most excavators judge an earthquake. Troy VIIa rebuilt on the same plan and ended in fire about 1200–1175 BCE; VIIb shows new, Balkan-influenced material. Hittite texts locate Wilusa in the far west of the Arzawa lands, reached via the Seha River land, which points to the Troad. From the Archaic period Greek Ilion reused the ruins as a sanctuary city; Hellenistic builders sheared off the top of the mound for the temple terrace of Athena, and Hellenistic and Roman foundations, stone robbing, erosion and ploughing removed much of the Bronze Age lower city. Schliemann then trenched through the mound looking for a burned Homeric city, and later teams used stratigraphy, magnetic prospection and radiocarbon dating to rebuild the sequence.
records.why_it_matters: Troy is where the archaeology of the Aegean and Anatolia was given a datable backbone: UNESCO describes the chronology established by its excavations as fundamental to understanding the region's Bronze Age, and Schliemann's work there is often taken as the start of modern archaeology and of its public appeal. Its Late Bronze Age citadel and probable identification with Wilusa make it a meeting point of the Hittite and Mycenaean worlds, documented in Hittite diplomacy rather than in Greek epic alone. Its legend had concrete political consequences: Xerxes and Alexander staged sacrifices there, and Strabo records that Julius Caesar, claiming descent from Aeneas, granted Ilion territory, freedom and exemption from taxes, while the Aeneid turned the Trojan story into Rome's founding myth. Its modern history carries a live dispute, because the Troy II gold taken from Berlin in 1945 is held in Moscow under a 1998 Russian law that Berlin calls a breach of international law. A counterfactual shows what was lost: Jablonka and Rose argue that a city exchanging letters with Hittite kings must have kept an archive. Had Hellenistic temple builders not levelled the citadel's summit, and had Schliemann not trenched through what remained, the palace area and perhaps written records might have survived to settle whether Wilusa and Homer's Troy were the same place.

perspectives.holder: The Tübingen–Cincinnati excavators (Korfmann; Jablonka and Rose 2004) and Easton, Hawkins, Sherratt and Sherratt (2002)
perspectives.account: Late Bronze Age Troy (late VI and VIIa) was a citadel of 2–3 ha with a fortified lower city of 25–35 ha, defended by a rock-cut ditch and palisade, by far the largest site in the Troad and the probable capital of Wilusa with a significant role in regional exchange.

perspectives.holder: Frank Kolb and Dieter Hertel (2001–2005)
perspectives.account: The lower city was only sparsely occupied in its middle and not at all in the south, the ditches were not defensive and were narrower than claimed, no lower-town wall has been shown, and the population should be put at 3,000 or even 1,000; Kolb also holds that Troy's trade role is unproven and that the reconstructions mix findings with assumption.

perspectives.holder: Hittitologists such as J. D. Hawkins and F. Starke (as reported by Easton et al. 2002), followed by Livius
perspectives.account: Hittite geography places the Arzawa kingdom of Wilusa in the Troad, and Hisarlık is the only site there of the right rank, so Wilusa is most probably Troy/Ilios; S. Heinhold-Krahmer treated this as unproven, and Hertel denied it.

perspectives.holder: Blegen's excavators and later analysts summarised by Rutter and Livius
perspectives.account: Troy VI was destroyed by an earthquake and Troy VIIa was sacked, but VIIa's fall came when Mycenaean palaces could hardly mount an overseas expedition, so the Iliad does not straightforwardly describe a datable event; Smithsonian Magazine instead reports a general view placing the epic's events at Hisarlık around 1180 BCE.

perspectives.holder: Strabo (1st century BCE), following Demetrius of Scepsis
perspectives.account: The Ilion of his day was not the site of Homer's Ilium when the poems' geography is taken at face value.

perspectives.holder: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (German position on 'Priam's Treasure')
perspectives.account: Schliemann gave the collection to Berlin in 1881; the Red Army took the gold as spoils of war in 1945; the 1998 Duma resolution declaring it Russian state property contravenes international law, and Berlin remains custodian of the collection under his bequest.

perspectives.holder: Russian museum and public view as reported in 1996 (Pushkin Museum exhibition)
perspectives.account: Many Russians regard the gold as legitimately taken spoils of victory over Nazi Germany; the Pushkin Museum put it on display from 15 April 1996 despite German objections.

records.title: Uruk (Warka)
records.summary: Uruk, the ruin field of Warka in southern Iraq, grew from a late-5th-millennium BCE settlement into perhaps the largest city of its age; its Eanna temple precinct yielded the oldest known writing, conventionally dated c. 3200 BCE.
records.card: Uruk lies in the desert of Iraq's Al-Muthanna Governorate, once on the edge of Euphrates marshes. In the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE) it held an estimated 20,000–50,000 people, temples on the Anu terrace and in the Eanna precinct, and the administrators who devised proto-cuneiform. Walled early in the 3rd millennium BCE, a wall later credited to Gilgamesh, it stayed inhabited into the 1st millennium CE and has been dug by German teams since 1912.
records.what:
Uruk is the ruin field known in Arabic as al-Warkāʾ, about 33 km east of As-Samawah in Iraq's Al-Muthanna Governorate. Its Sumerian name was Unug; Greek sources called it Orchoē, and it is also known as Erech. The city stood southwest of an ancient Euphrates channel, now dry, at the edge of freshwater marshes, with canals running through its quarters; the river's later shift away from the site was a key factor in its decline.

Settlement began around the end of the 5th millennium BCE, at the close of the Ubaid period, and grew through the 4th millennium, the span archaeologists call the Uruk period after this site. In the Late Uruk phase (c. 3350–3100 BCE) Uruk covered roughly 2.5 km², nearly twice the next largest settlement, and housed an estimated 20,000 to 50,000 people. In the west, a terrace raised at least ten times to about 12 m, the so-called Anu Ziggurat, carried the White Temple, a whitewashed hall of about 22 by 17.5 m whose construction is radiocarbon-dated to 3517–3358 BCE. To the east lay Eanna, precinct of the goddess Inanna, where about 5,000 proto-cuneiform tablets, the oldest known writing, were recovered, nearly all from rubbish used as building fill. Facades of the period's great mudbrick buildings were studded with painted clay cones set in mosaic patterns.

Early in the 3rd millennium BCE a mudbrick wall up to 5 m thick, with semicircular bastions, was built round the city; later tradition credited it to King Gilgamesh. Published figures for the city's size differ, from 2.5 km² to more than 6 km² and from 9.8 km to about 11 km of wall, because they describe different phases and methods. Uruk stayed a religious centre for millennia: a ziggurat was raised in Eanna about 4,200 years ago, the Seleucid-period city had great sanctuaries such as the Bit Resh of Anu and Antum and the Irigal of Ishtar, and a temple was built under Parthian rule. Occupation continued into the late Sasanian period (7th century CE). German teams have excavated the site since 1912, and in 2016 it was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage property The Ahwar of Southern Iraq.

End: ICOMOS gives the late Sasanian period, 7th century CE (printed '7rd'); the Artefacts/DAI reconstruction project says only 'to the 1st millennium CE'. The end year 650 is the midpoint of the 7th century, not an attested abandonment date.

records.how: Uruk grew on a marshy deltaic plain where the Euphrates, its channels and freshwater marshes supplied water, fish, reeds and fertile soil. Canals ran through the city from north to south, linking quarters to river traffic and watering gardens inside the walls. During the 4th millennium BCE the population swelled and institutions centred on the temple precincts came to control large stores of goods and labour; keeping track of production, rations and workers led administrators in Eanna to draw signs on clay, first with curved incised lines (Uruk IV) and about a century later with impressed, straightened strokes (Uruk III). The same script then appears at Jemdet Nasr, Khafajah and Tell Uqair, so the technique spread quickly through Babylonia. Builders worked almost wholly in earth: sun-dried earth blocks laid in mud mortar, horizontal layers of bitumen mortar as waterproofing in the Anu terrace, reed-mat reinforcement layers in the later Eanna ziggurat (about 11.5 million blocks), white lime paint on the White Temple and painted clay-cone mosaics on facades. The terrace that carried the White Temple was rebuilt and raised at least ten times. Early in the 3rd millennium a double ring of mudbrick wall with some burnt brick enclosed the city. Long-term decline followed the drying of the marshes after about 2000 BCE and the river's change of course, though the temples were rebuilt in Seleucid and Parthian times.
records.why_it_matters: Uruk is the clearest case in the archaeological record of a society crossing into urban life. Its administrators produced the oldest known writing, a bookkeeping system for grain, livestock, labour and rations; that script developed into cuneiform, which was later adapted to write Akkadian, Eblaite, Elamite, Hittite and other languages across the ancient Middle East and was still written in the 1st century CE, more than three thousand years after its invention. The city's scale, temple institutions, monumental mudbrick architecture and canal network set the pattern for the Sumerian city-states that followed, and objects in Uruk style reached from central Iran to the Nile Delta before about 3000 BCE. Uruk also supplied the setting of Mesopotamian literary memory: the Epic of Gilgamesh, among the earliest works of literature, centres on its king and his wall, and the Sumerian poem Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta claims the city invented writing. If the Eanna rubbish fills had not preserved some 5,000 archaic tablets, the earliest stage of writing would be known only from the slightly later Uruk III-type tablets found at northern Babylonian sites, and historians would have far weaker evidence that writing began as administration rather than literature. The site also shows how fragile early cities were: when the marshes dried and the Euphrates moved away, Uruk shrank to a sanctuary town and finally emptied. Today its eroding mudbrick ruins are part of Iraq's World Heritage property, conserved by Iraqi and German teams who still depend on clay from the region's canals to repair them.

records.title: Han dynasty
records.summary: The Han dynasty ruled a unified Chinese empire from 206 BCE to 220 CE, first from Chang'an and, after Wang Mang's Xin interregnum (9–23 CE), from Luoyang. Its census of 2 CE registered about 59.6 million people.
records.card: After the Qin empire broke apart in civil war, Liu Bang founded the Han, which held the Qin unification together for four centuries. Under Emperor Wu it pushed into Central Asia, Korea and the far south, while envoys such as Zhang Qian opened the routes later called the Silk Roads. Rebellion from 184 CE emptied the throne of real power, and the last emperor abdicated to Cao Pi of Wei in 220.
records.what:
The Han dynasty (漢 Hàn) was the ruling house of the Chinese empire for most of the four centuries after the Qin collapse. Liu Bang, a rebel commander, entered the Qin heartland in the first year of his reckoning (206 BCE), was made King of Han over Ba, Shu and Hanzhong by Xiang Yu, defeated Xiang Yu, and took the imperial title in 202 BCE. His capital, Chang'an in present-day Shaanxi, grew into a planned city with palaces, residential wards and two markets.

The Western (Former) Han reached its widest extent under Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE), who fought the Xiongnu steppe empire, sent Zhang Qian west to look for allies, retook southern China and northern Vietnam, founded commanderies in Korea, and in 101 BCE conquered Ferghana. A register compiled for 2 CE counted 103 commanderies and kingdoms, 1,314 counties, 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 people.

Feuding factions, among them the families of imperial consorts, weakened the Western Han. In 9 CE Wang Mang, who had governed as acting emperor, dropped the Han name and proclaimed his own Xin dynasty; he was killed when rebel troops stormed the palace at Chang'an in 23 CE. Liu Xiu, a ninth-generation descendant of Liu Bang, took the throne in 25 CE as Emperor Guangwu and made Luoyang his capital, opening the Eastern (Later) Han. Ban Chao restored Han power in Central Asia between 73 and 94 CE, and in 105 CE the court eunuch Cai Lun presented an improved method of making paper.

After 168 CE, struggles between palace eunuchs and the great families weakened the court. In 184 CE Zhang Jue's Yellow Turban followers rose on a single day, and in 216 the general Cao Cao raised himself to King of Wei. The last emperor, Liu Xie (Emperor Xian), abdicated in favour of Cao Cao's son Cao Pi in 220 CE, and the empire divided among Wei, Shu-Han and Wu.

Sources disagree on where to put the dynasty's start and end: museum and teaching timelines begin it in 206 BCE, when Liu Bang's reign years start, others at his enthronement in 202 BCE, and Michael Loewe treats the revolt of 184 CE rather than the abdication of 220 as the real end of Han imperial authority.

uncertainty.note: Start: 206 BCE (astronomical -205) is the conventional date (Met, Columbia), the first year of Liu Bang's reckoning in the Hanshu; he took the imperial title in his fifth year, 202 BCE (-201). The Hanshu year 1 opens with the tenth month, because the Qin-style year began in the tenth month, so its first months fall before January of 206 BCE. End: formal abdication in 220 CE; Loewe treats the Yellow Turban revolt of 184 CE as the effective end of imperial authority. The Xin interregnum (9–23 CE) and the civil war to 25 CE fall inside the span but were not Han rule.

records.how: The Han grew out of the civil war that followed the First Emperor's death in 210 BCE. Liu Bang reached the Qin capital region first, accepted the surrender of the last Qin ruler, was assigned the kingdom of Han in the southwest by Xiang Yu, and then fought Xiang Yu for the whole realm, taking the imperial title in 202 BCE. The dynasty held the boundaries Qin had set and governed through commanderies and counties together with subordinate kingdoms and marquisates, all four of which the register of 2 CE still lists. Emperor Wu made Confucian learning the basis of official conduct and education, so the bureaucracy came to rely on men trained in the classics. Against the Xiongnu he sent armies north and envoys west: Zhang Qian, setting out with over a hundred men during the Jianyuan era (140–134 BCE), returned about thirteen years later with only two, but with knowledge of Ferghana, Sogdiana and Bactria. Posthouses and beacon towers along the Hexi Corridor and the conquest of Ferghana in 101 BCE gave the Han control of routes around the Taklamakan, and the Ferghana campaign brought in prized cavalry horses, while silk and gold went west in exchange for wine, spices, woollens, grapes, pomegranates and alfalfa. The Western Han weakened as factions, including consort families, fought for power, and Wang Mang, after ruling as acting emperor, took the throne in 9 CE. After his death in 23 CE, Liu Xiu restored the house at Luoyang. In the second century, rivalry between eunuchs and leading families divided the court after Emperor Huan died without a designated heir in 168. The Yellow Turban rising of 184, whose organised followers the Hou Hanshu puts at 360,000, prompted the court to put He Jin in command of the armies; Loewe sees this revolt as the end of real imperial authority. In the years that followed, the general Cao Cao rose to be King of Wei in 216, and his son Cao Pi received the abdication in 220.
records.why_it_matters: The Han turned the short-lived Qin unification into a lasting form of state. Its borders, inherited from Qin and held for four centuries, roughly outline the China of later history, and Michael Loewe notes that the centralised imperial model it created went largely unchallenged for some two thousand years, until the late nineteenth century. Several of its institutions outlived it directly. Emperor Wu's choice of Confucian learning as the basis of official conduct and schooling shaped the training of Chinese officials for many centuries, and Sima Qian's Shiji set the model for the official dynastic histories, including the Hanshu and Hou Hanshu used in this record. Its register of 2 CE, preserved commandery by commandery in the Hanshu, records nearly 60 million registered people in over 12 million households. Han envoys, the Ferghana campaign and the relay posts of the Hexi Corridor helped the long-distance exchange that UNESCO says grew sharply from the 2nd century BCE, carrying Chinese silk west and bringing grapes and alfalfa east. Paper, made in a cruder form in the Western Han and improved in the method Cai Lun presented in 105 CE, came into general use in the empire, according to the Hou Hanshu. A counterfactual shows what was at stake: had the civil war after 210 BCE ended in lasting division among rival kings, as Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE proposed, the idea of a single Chinese empire might never have hardened into the norm. The Han's collapse after 184 CE, and the division into rival kingdoms that followed, show how much that unity depended on the dynasty holding together.

related.title: Qin dynasty
related.because: The civil war that broke out after the First Emperor's death in 210 BCE destroyed the Qin regime, and Liu Bang's victory in it produced the Han, which maintained the boundaries Qin had established.

related.title: Silk Roads: Chang'an–Tianshan Corridor
related.because: Han envoys, the conquest of Ferghana in 101 BCE and a state system of posthouses and beacon towers secured the routes linking Chang'an to Central Asia, along which long-distance trade in silk expanded from the 2nd century BCE.

related.title: Cai Lun presents improved papermaking to the Han court
Three Kingdoms period
related.because: When Emperor Xian abdicated to Cao Pi in 220 CE, Wei claimed the succession and the former Han territory divided among the rival states of Wei, Shu-Han and Wu.

beats.action: marker.pin { at: [34.3044, 108.8572], label: 'Liu Bang, King of Han' }
beats.caption: 206 BCE: in the civil war after the Qin collapse, Liu Bang takes the Qin heartland and is made King of Han; his reign years start here.

beats.action: region.fill { source: chgis-v6-pref-pgn, snapshot: -201, label: 'Han empire' }
beats.caption: 202 BCE: Liu Bang takes the imperial title. Chang'an becomes the capital of a reunited empire.

beats.action: region.morph { from: 'Han empire 143 BCE', to: 'Han empire 108 BCE' }
beats.caption: Under Emperor Wu (141–87 BCE) the empire expands into the far south, northern Vietnam and Korea while fighting the Xiongnu.

beats.span: departure within -139 / -133 (Jianyuan era), return about 13 years later
beats.action: path.trace { from: [34.3044, 108.8572], via: ['Ferghana', 'Sogdiana', 'Bactria'], label: 'Zhang Qian' }
beats.caption: Zhang Qian sets out west with over a hundred men; held by the Xiongnu for over ten years, he returns about thirteen years later with one companion.

beats.action: flow.arc { from: [34.3044, 108.8572], to: 'Ferghana', goods: ['silk', 'gold'], return: ['horses', 'wine', 'grapes', 'alfalfa'] }
beats.caption: After Ferghana is conquered in 101 BCE, the Han controls the routes around the Taklamakan; silk goes west, cavalry horses and new crops come east.

beats.action: numbers.counter { field: registered_population, value: 59594978, households: 12233062 }
beats.caption: 2 CE: the register counts 59,594,978 people in 12,233,062 households across 103 commanderies and kingdoms.

beats.action: region.hatch { label: 'Xin dynasty of Wang Mang' }
beats.caption: 9 CE: the regent Wang Mang drops the Han name and founds Xin. He is killed when rebels storm Chang'an in 23 CE.

beats.action: camera.fly { to: [34.7311, 112.6214], label: 'Luoyang' }
beats.caption: 25 CE: Liu Xiu restores the Han as Emperor Guangwu and makes Luoyang, about 350 km east of Chang'an, the capital.

beats.action: marker.pin { at: [34.7311, 112.6214], label: 'Cai Lun presents papermaking' }
beats.caption: 105 CE: Cai Lun presents paper made from bark, hemp, rags and old nets; it comes into general use across the empire.

beats.action: region.pulse { label: 'Yellow Turban rising', intensity: 1.0 }
beats.caption: 184 CE: Zhang Jue's Yellow Turbans rise on a single day; after this, real power passes from the throne to generals.

beats.action: region.split { into: ['Wei', 'Shu-Han', 'Wu'] }
beats.caption: 220 CE: the last Han emperor abdicates to Cao Pi of Wei, and the empire divides into three rival kingdoms.

perspectives.holder: Metropolitan Museum of Art; Columbia University Asia for Educators; Hanshu reign-year reckoning
perspectives.account: The dynasty begins in 206 BCE, the first year of Liu Bang's reign count, when he took the Qin heartland and was made King of Han.

perspectives.holder: Dating by imperial enthronement (Hanshu, Annals of Gaozu)
perspectives.account: Liu Bang became emperor only in his fifth year, 202 BCE, after defeating Xiang Yu; on this reading Han rule over a unified empire starts then.

perspectives.holder: Michael Loewe, Cambridge History of China vol. 1 (1986)
perspectives.account: The formal end is Emperor Xian's abdication in 220 CE, but imperial authority had in effect collapsed with the Yellow Turban revolt of 184 CE, leaving a powerless emperor on the throne.

perspectives.holder: Hou Hanshu (5th century CE), the traditional account
perspectives.account: Cai Lun devised paper from bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets and presented it in 105 CE; the empire called it 'Marquis Cai's paper'.

perspectives.holder: Archaeological finds: Fangmatan tomb 5 (Gansu) and Western Han sites; Li Xiaocen (2016), with doubts from Chen Gang
perspectives.account: Paper was already used in the Western Han, roughly 250 years before Cai Lun, who improved rather than invented it; whether the Fangmatan fragment counts as true paper is still debated.

perspectives.holder: Hans Bielenstein, Cambridge History of China vol. 1 (1986)
perspectives.account: Traditional histories judge Wang Mang through the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven as a usurper, which makes a fair assessment of his reign difficult.

numbers.label: Registered population of the empire (register of 2 CE, Hanshu Treatise on Geography)
numbers.note: Single figure as recorded in the Hanshu. It is a registered count, not a modern estimate of total population; the commandery entries are dated Yuanshi 2 (src-hanshu-28a). Secondary works also cite a lower total of about 57.7 million, but no source I opened gave or explained it, so it is not used here.

numbers.label: Registered households (2 CE)
numbers.note: Single figure as recorded in the Hanshu totals.

numbers.label: Area of Eastern Han Luoyang
numbers.note: The Met gives about four square miles (≈10.4 km²); each of its two palace complexes covered about 125 acres (≈51 ha).

numbers.label: Followers of Zhang Jue at the rising of 184 CE, as claimed
numbers.note: A traditional figure for his organised followers (部師三十六萬), not a count; the commentary cites the Xu Hanshu for 'over 360,000'.

records.audience_note: Mentions war, rebellion and violent deaths (the killing of Wang Mang in 23 CE, frontier wars with the Xiongnu) without graphic description.

importance.justification: One of the largest states of the ancient world, ruling tens of millions of people for four centuries, it fixed the model of the unified Chinese empire and its official historiography, so it must be visible at whole-planet view.
